meta.rendering_note: All mathematical expressions are wrapped in KaTeX inline-math delimiters \( ... \), including vector notation (\vec{F}), fractions, and any exponent attached to a unit (e.g. 10 m/s\(^2\)); no raw Unicode math symbols (such as arrows, root signs, or the degree sign) appear outside these delimiters. topics.name: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
topics.summary: Newton's first law states that a body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by a net external force; this tendency to resist a change in motion is called inertia, and it depends only on mass. Newton's second law quantifies how force changes motion: the net force on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum, \( \vec{F}_{net}=\dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt} \), which for constant mass simplifies to the familiar \( \vec{F}_{net}=m\vec{a} \). Momentum, \( \vec{p}=m\vec{v} \), is a vector quantity, so both its magnitude and direction matter when force or momentum change is being analyzed. This topic covers single-body dynamics: drawing a correct free-body diagram, identifying every real force acting on one object, and applying \( F_{net}=ma \) along a chosen direction to solve for acceleration, unknown forces, or motion parameters like velocity, time, or distance in problems involving lifts, blocks on surfaces, and objects under multiple simultaneous forces.
topics.worked_example: A 5 kg block on a frictionless floor is pushed by a horizontal 20 N force while a second, opposing horizontal force of 5 N also acts on it. The net force is \( 20-5=15 \) N, so the acceleration is \( a=\dfrac{15}{5}=3 \) m/s\(^2\), in the direction of the larger force.
common_mistakes: Treating momentum as a scalar and forgetting that a change in direction alone changes momentum even if speed stays constant
Applying \( F=ma \) using only part of the forces acting on a body, or a force that acts on a different body entirely
Confusing mass, a constant measure of inertia, with weight, a force \( mg \) that depends on \( g \)
Forgetting that \( F=ma \) uses the net force, not any single applied force, when other forces are also present

topics.name: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
topics.summary: Newton's third law states that whenever one body exerts a force on a second body, the second body exerts an equal-magnitude, oppositely-directed force of the same fundamental nature back on the first. The two forces in this pair always act on two different bodies, never on the same one, and they never cancel each other out when analyzing the motion of a single object — only forces acting on that one object are relevant to its own equation of motion. This topic also covers conservation of linear momentum: for an isolated system experiencing zero net external force, the total momentum before and after any interaction, such as a collision, explosion, or recoil, remains constant, even though internal forces between the system's parts, governed by the third law, can be large. A key subtlety is that whether a force counts as internal or external depends entirely on how the system's boundary is drawn — a string's tension is internal when analyzing the whole connected system together, but becomes an external force the moment attention narrows to just one block within that system.
key_formulas: \( \sum \vec{p}_{i,initial}=\sum \vec{p}_{i,final} \) for an isolated system (zero net external force)
topics.worked_example: A 60 kg person standing at rest on frictionless ice throws a 2 kg ball forward at 15 m/s. Since the total momentum was initially zero, the person recoils backward with momentum \( 2\times15=30 \) kg m/s, giving a recoil speed of \( \dfrac{30}{60}=0.5 \) m/s.
common_mistakes: Pairing a normal force on an object with that same object's own weight and calling them an action-reaction pair, when both act on the same body
Believing action-reaction pairs can cancel each other out for the motion of a single object, when they actually act on two different bodies
Applying momentum conservation while a genuine external force, such as friction from the ground, is still acting on the system
Treating a connecting force such as string tension as always internal, regardless of which system boundary is being analyzed

topics.name: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
topics.summary: A particle is in equilibrium when the net force acting on it is zero, so it remains at rest or moves with constant velocity. This topic covers the everyday contact and constraint forces that commonly appear in equilibrium and connected-body problems: the normal force, perpendicular to a contact surface and adjusting to whatever value equilibrium or the second law requires rather than being fixed to the object's weight; tension in light, inextensible strings, uniform throughout an ideal massless string and over an ideal massless, frictionless pulley; and the spring force given by Hooke's law, \( F=-kx \), where the restoring force is proportional to the displacement from the spring's natural length. Connected-body problems, such as a block and a hanging mass joined by a string over a pulley, require treating each body's forces separately, or, for finding acceleration, treating the whole system together, and are a frequent source of errors when tension is mistakenly treated as a fixed, known quantity rather than found from the equations of motion.
topics.worked_example: Two blocks of mass 2 kg and 3 kg are connected by a string over a smooth pulley (an Atwood machine). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the acceleration is \( a=\dfrac{(3-2)\times10}{2+3}=2 \) m/s\(^2\), and the tension is \( T=\dfrac{2\times2\times3\times10}{5}=24 \) N.
common_mistakes: Assuming the normal force always equals \( mg \), even when other vertical forces, like an applied force or an incline, are also present
Treating the tension throughout a connected system as simply equal to a hanging weight, rather than solving the full equations of motion
Using \( F=kx \) with the object's total distance from a fixed point rather than its displacement, extension or compression, from the spring's natural length
Forgetting that a string can only pull, never push, and mistakenly allowing a negative tension in a solution

topics.name: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
topics.summary: Friction is the force that opposes relative sliding, or the tendency to slide, between two surfaces in contact. Static friction acts when there is no relative sliding, and it is self-adjusting: it automatically takes on whatever value, up to a maximum of \( f_{s,max}=\mu_sN \), is needed to prevent relative motion — it is not automatically equal to this maximum value. Once an object actually starts sliding, kinetic friction takes over, with a roughly constant magnitude \( f_k=\mu_kN \), and typically \( \mu_k<\mu_s \) for a given pair of surfaces. A related idea is the angle of repose: the maximum angle of an incline at which an object placed on it will just remain at rest without sliding, given by \( \tan\theta=\mu_s \), since at this critical angle, the maximum available static friction exactly balances the weight component along the slope. This topic covers a wide range of scenarios: blocks on horizontal and inclined surfaces, connected bodies experiencing friction, and problems requiring careful reasoning about which friction regime actually applies.
topics.worked_example: A 4 kg block rests on a horizontal floor with \( \mu_s=0.5 \), \( \mu_k=0.4 \). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the maximum static friction is \( 0.5\times4\times10=20 \) N. A 12 N horizontal push does not exceed this, so the block stays at rest, and the actual friction on it is exactly 12 N, not 20 N.
common_mistakes: Assuming static friction always equals its maximum value \( \mu_sN \), rather than only whatever value is actually needed to prevent sliding
Using \( \mu_k \) in a situation where the object has not actually started sliding, or vice versa
Forgetting that the normal force \( N \) used in the friction formula may itself depend on other forces present, such as an applied force with a vertical component
Mixing up \( \mu_s \) and \( \mu_k \) values in a problem that gives both, especially when checking whether an object starts to move at all

topics.name: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
topics.summary: Centripetal force is not a distinct, separate type of force — it is simply the name given to whichever net real force, such as tension, gravity, friction, a component of the normal force, or some combination, happens to point toward the center of a circular path and supplies the acceleration \( a_c=v^2/r \) needed to keep an object moving along that curved path. A common and serious error is adding an extra centripetal-force arrow to a free-body diagram alongside the real forces that are already providing it, which double-counts the same physical force. This topic covers flat and banked curves, where for a frictionless banked curve at the optimum speed \( v=\sqrt{rg\tan\theta} \), and with friction, distinct formulas give the maximum and minimum safe speeds, conical pendulums, and single-point force-balance problems at the top and bottom of vertical circles. Banking works by tilting the road so that part of the normal force itself points toward the center, reducing or eliminating the need for friction to supply the turning force.
key_formulas: Vertical circle — top: \( mg+T=\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \); bottom: \( T-mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \)
topics.worked_example: A car takes a frictionless banked curve of radius 40 m, banked at \( 45° \) (\( \tan45°=1 \)). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the optimum speed is \( v=\sqrt{40\times10\times1}=\sqrt{400}=20 \) m/s.
common_mistakes: Adding a separate centripetal force to a free-body diagram in addition to the real force that is already supplying it
Using the frictionless banking formula \( v=\sqrt{rg\tan\theta} \) even when friction is present and relevant to the problem
Forgetting to include the object's weight alongside the centripetal force term when finding tension or normal force at the top or bottom of a vertical circle
Assuming centripetal force is only relevant for perfectly circular, constant-speed motion, rather than recognizing it as the center-directed component of the net force in any curved motion

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A passenger standing in a bus lurches forward when the bus suddenly stops. Which property of matter causes this?
options: Inertia of motion of the passenger's body
Newton's third law reaction from the bus floor
The passenger's momentum is destroyed by air resistance
Centripetal force acting on the passenger
questions.explanation:
Newton's first law states a body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by a net external force.

Before the bus stops, the passenger's body is moving forward at the bus's speed.

When the bus stops suddenly, the passenger's feet stop with the floor (friction acts on the feet), but the upper body has no such force acting on it instantly, so it continues moving forward due to inertia of motion, causing the lurch.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to a body's velocity when no net force acts on it, and what resists a change in that velocity.
distractor_logic: Mixes in the third law, which explains paired contact forces, not why the body resists a change in its own state of motion.
Air resistance is negligible here and momentum is not "destroyed"; this is not the relevant force.
There is no circular motion in this situation, so centripetal force is irrelevant.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: Newton's first law of motion is most directly a qualitative definition of which physical quantity?
options: Mass, as the quantity of matter contained in a body
Force, as whatever changes a body's state of rest or uniform motion
Momentum, as the product of mass and velocity
Weight, as the gravitational pull on a body
questions.explanation:
Newton's first law says a body's velocity does not change unless a net external force acts on it.

This makes the law a qualitative definition of force: force is precisely the physical cause that changes a body's state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line.

Mass and momentum only enter once the second law is stated quantitatively.
questions.hint: Ask what the first law says must be present in order for a body's velocity to change.
distractor_logic: Mass is defined quantitatively through the ratio \( F/a \) in the second law, not by the first law.
Momentum is introduced when the second law is stated quantitatively, not by the qualitative first law.
Weight is one specific force due to gravity; it is not what the first law is defining.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: What is the SI unit of linear momentum?
questions.explanation:
Linear momentum is defined as \( p=mv \).

Mass has the SI unit kg and velocity has the SI unit m/s.

Multiplying these gives the SI unit of momentum as kg m/s (equivalently N s, since force times time also gives kg m/s).
questions.hint: Recall momentum is mass times velocity, and build its unit from the base units of mass and velocity.
distractor_logic: This is the unit of force (from \( F=ma \)), not momentum.
This combination of units corresponds to force (since \( 1\text{ N}=1\text{ kg m/s}^2 \)), not momentum.
The joule is the SI unit of energy or work, which has different dimensions from momentum.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A body of mass 4 kg moves with a velocity of 5 m/s. What is the magnitude of its linear momentum?
questions.explanation:
Linear momentum is given by \( p=mv \).

Substituting \( m=4 \) kg and \( v=5 \) m/s gives \( p=4\times5=20 \) kg m/s.
questions.hint: Momentum is the product, not the sum or ratio, of mass and velocity.
distractor_logic: Adds the mass and velocity values instead of multiplying them.
Divides velocity by mass instead of multiplying mass by velocity.
Divides mass by velocity instead of multiplying mass by velocity.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A net force of 15 N acts on a body of mass 3 kg. What acceleration does the body experience?
questions.explanation:
Newton's second law gives \( F=ma \), so \( a=\dfrac{F}{m} \).

Substituting \( F=15 \) N and \( m=3 \) kg gives \( a=\dfrac{15}{3}=5 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: Rearrange Newton's second law to solve for acceleration.
distractor_logic: Multiplies force by mass instead of dividing force by mass.
Adds force and mass instead of applying \( a=F/m \).
Inverts the ratio, computing \( m/F \) instead of \( F/m \).

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: Which statement most precisely expresses Newton's second law of motion?
options: The net force on a body equals its mass divided by its acceleration
The net external force on a body equals the time rate of change of its linear momentum, \( \vec{F}=\dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt} \)
The net force on a body is proportional to its displacement
The net force on a body equals the rate of change of its kinetic energy
questions.explanation:
Newton's second law states that the net external force acting on a body equals the time rate of change of its linear momentum: \( \vec{F}=\dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt} \).

For constant mass, this reduces to the familiar \( \vec{F}=m\vec{a} \), since \( \dfrac{d(mv)}{dt}=m\dfrac{dv}{dt}=ma \) when \( m \) does not change.
questions.hint: The most general form of the second law is written in terms of momentum, not just mass times acceleration.
distractor_logic: This inverts the correct relationship; force is mass times acceleration, not mass divided by acceleration.
This describes a spring-like restoring force, not the general statement of the second law.
Rate of change of kinetic energy is related to power delivered by the force, not to the second law's momentum statement.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A book lies at rest on a table and stays at rest indefinitely. According to Newton's first law, this happens because
options: the book has no mass and therefore cannot move
gravity is switched off for objects in equilibrium
the net external force acting on the book is zero
the book's inertia actively pushes it downward against the table
questions.explanation:
The book has two forces on it: gravity pulling it down and the normal force from the table pushing it up.

These are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so the net external force on the book is zero.

By Newton's first law, a body under zero net force continues in its existing state of rest (or uniform motion), so the book stays at rest.
questions.hint: Zero net force does not mean zero forces are present — think about what balances what.
distractor_logic: The book clearly has mass; having mass is unrelated to why it stays at rest.
Gravity continues to act on the book; it is balanced by the normal force, not absent.
Inertia is a resistance to a change in motion, not an active force that pushes anything.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A puck slides on a frictionless horizontal surface and no horizontal force acts on it after it is given an initial push. What happens to its velocity?
options: It gradually decreases to zero because no force is sustaining it
It increases steadily because inertia keeps accelerating the puck
It changes direction periodically while its magnitude stays fixed
It remains constant in both magnitude and direction
questions.explanation:
Newton's first law states that in the absence of a net external force, a body continues in uniform motion in a straight line.

Since the surface is frictionless and no other horizontal force acts, the net force on the puck is zero.

Its velocity vector — both speed and direction — therefore remains unchanged.
questions.hint: With truly zero net force, ask what Newton's first law says must happen to velocity — not just speed.
distractor_logic: This is the pre-Newtonian misconception that motion requires a continuously applied force; a net force is needed only to change velocity, not to maintain it.
Inertia is a resistance to a change in velocity, not a cause of acceleration.
With zero net force there is no cause for the direction to change either.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: Newton's third law of motion states that
options: for every action force, there is a reaction force equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on a different body
for every force there is an equal and opposite force acting on the same body, so the net force on any body is always zero
the total force on a system increases when internal forces act between its parts
action and reaction forces act simultaneously on the same body but in different directions
questions.explanation:
Newton's third law states that whenever one body exerts a force on a second body (the action), the second body exerts an equal and opposite force on the first (the reaction).

The key feature often missed is that the two forces act on two different bodies — never on the same body — so they can never cancel to give zero net force on a single object.

This is why action-reaction pairs never appear together in a single free-body diagram of one object.
questions.hint: Action-reaction pairs act on two different bodies, never on the same one.
distractor_logic: This is the central misconception about the third law; action-reaction pairs act on two different bodies and can never combine to cancel the net force on a single one of them.
Internal forces between parts of a system always cancel in pairs by the third law; they never increase the system's total force.
Action and reaction forces act on two different bodies, not on the same body.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: A book rests on a table. What is the true Newton's third-law reaction to the normal force that the table exerts upward on the book?
options: The weight of the book, acting downward on the book itself
The force the book exerts downward on the table
The friction force the table exerts on the book
The force of gravity the book exerts on the Earth
questions.explanation:
The normal force is the table pushing up on the book.

By Newton's third law, the true reaction is the book pushing down on the table, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, and acting on the table (not on the book).

The book's weight is a separate, unrelated gravitational force that happens to be equal in magnitude to the normal force only because the book is in vertical equilibrium — it is not the third-law reaction pair to the normal force.
questions.hint: The reaction to a normal force must be of the same nature (a contact/normal-type force) and must act on the object exerting the original force — here, the table.
distractor_logic: This pairs a normal force with a gravitational force on the same body (the book); different force types acting on the same body can never be a third-law pair.
This is a different type of force, and here it is not even the relevant force being paired with the normal force.
This is a genuine third-law pair, but to the book's own weight, not to the table's normal force on the book.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: For an isolated system of two colliding bodies (no external forces act), which quantity remains constant throughout the collision?
options: The individual momentum of each body separately
The total kinetic energy of the system
The total linear momentum of the two-body system
questions.explanation:
When no net external force acts on a system, its total linear momentum remains constant, even though the two bodies exert internal forces on each other during the collision.

Each body's individual momentum generally changes (since it experiences an internal force from the other body), but these changes are equal and opposite by Newton's third law, so their sum is unchanged.

Kinetic energy, by contrast, is conserved only in elastic collisions, not in general.
questions.hint: Momentum conservation applies to the system's total momentum, not to each body's momentum individually.
distractor_logic: Each body's own momentum generally changes during the collision, since it experiences an internal force from the other body.
This is true only for elastic collisions, not for collisions in general.
The velocities of the individual bodies change as a result of the collision forces.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: A gun of mass M, initially at rest, fires a bullet of mass m forward with speed v. Which principle directly explains why the gun recoils backward?
options: Newton's first law, since a body at rest must remain at rest
Conservation of kinetic energy of the (gun + bullet) system
The bullet's weight acting on the gun as a reaction force
Conservation of the total momentum of the (gun + bullet) system, which was initially zero
questions.explanation:
Before firing, the (gun+bullet) system is at rest, so its total momentum is zero.

The explosive force between gun and bullet is purely internal to the system, so it cannot change the system's total momentum.

Therefore the bullet's forward momentum must be exactly balanced by an equal and opposite backward momentum of the gun, causing the recoil.
questions.hint: The internal forces between gun and bullet are equal and opposite, so the total momentum of the system — initially zero — must stay zero.
distractor_logic: This misapplies the first law; the gun does not remain at rest once it fires, since a force does act on it.
Kinetic energy is not conserved here; energy stored before firing converts into the kinetic energy of both gun and bullet.
Weight is a gravitational force on the bullet itself and has no third-law connection to the gun's recoil.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: Which of the following is a genuine Newton's third-law action-reaction pair?
options: The force of Earth's gravity pulling a falling apple down, and the force of the apple's gravity pulling Earth up
The weight of a hanging lamp, and the tension in the string holding it up
The normal force on a box from the floor, and the friction force on the box from the floor
The push a swimmer exerts on the water, and the buoyant force the water exerts back on the swimmer
questions.explanation:
Earth's gravitational pull on the apple and the apple's equal and opposite gravitational pull on Earth are both gravitational forces, equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on two different bodies (apple and Earth) — a genuine third-law pair.

The other options each pair two different types of force acting on the same single body, or two dissimilar effects, which by definition cannot be an action-reaction pair.

Recognizing that a valid pair must match in force-type, not merely appear equal and opposite, is essential to avoid this common trap.
questions.hint: A true third-law pair must be of the same type of force, equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on two different bodies — check each candidate pair against all of these conditions.
distractor_logic: Both forces act on the same body (the lamp) and are of different natures (gravity vs. tension); this is an equilibrium pair, not a third-law pair.
Both forces act on the same body (the box) and are different types of force; this cannot be a third-law pair.
These are two different types of force (a propulsive push versus buoyancy), so they cannot be a matched third-law pair even though both involve the swimmer and the water.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: Two forces form a genuine Newton's third-law pair. On how many distinct bodies do these two forces act, in total?
options: One — both forces act on the same single body
Two — one force acts on each of the two interacting bodies
Three — the two bodies plus the medium connecting them
It depends on whether the bodies are in contact or not
questions.explanation:
By Newton's third law, if body A exerts a force on body B, then body B exerts an equal and opposite force on body A.

These two forces always act on two distinct bodies — one on each — regardless of whether the interaction is a contact force (like a push) or a non-contact force (like gravity).

A pair of forces acting on the same single body can never be an action-reaction pair, no matter how equal and opposite they may appear.
questions.hint: Every genuine action-reaction pair involves exactly two bodies — the force never appears twice on the same object.
distractor_logic: This is exactly the central misconception about the third law; the two forces of a genuine pair never act on the same body.
This invents an unnecessary third body; third-law pairs are defined for exactly two interacting bodies.
Contact is irrelevant; third-law pairs exist for both contact forces and non-contact forces (like gravity), always acting on the same two interacting bodies.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: Two identical carts, each of mass 5 kg, are initially at rest and pushed apart by a compressed spring between them (no external horizontal force). After the spring releases, cart A moves at 2 m/s to the left. What is the speed of cart B?
questions.explanation:
Before the spring releases, the total momentum of the (cart A + cart B) system is zero, and no external horizontal force acts.

So the total momentum stays zero afterward: \( m_Av_A+m_Bv_B=0 \).

With equal masses, \( v_B=-v_A \), so cart B moves at 2 m/s in the direction opposite to cart A — that is, 2 m/s to the right.
questions.hint: The system's total momentum starts at zero and must stay at zero — use this to relate the two carts' final momenta.
distractor_logic: This assumes both carts move in the same direction, which would violate conservation of the system's zero total momentum.
This incorrectly halves cart A's speed for cart B, instead of recognizing that with equal masses and zero initial momentum, the speeds must be equal in magnitude.
This incorrectly doubles cart A's speed for cart B, rather than equating the magnitudes of the two carts' momenta.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: The law of conservation of linear momentum for a system of particles holds strictly whenever
options: all the particles in the system are moving with constant velocity
there are no internal forces acting between the particles of the system
the total kinetic energy of the system stays constant
the net external force acting on the system is zero
questions.explanation:
Newton's second law applied to a system gives \( \vec{F}_{net,ext}=\dfrac{d\vec{p}_{total}}{dt} \).

Internal forces between particles always occur in equal-and-opposite third-law pairs and cancel out of this sum, so they never affect the total momentum.

Therefore, the total momentum of the system stays constant precisely when the net external force is zero — regardless of how large or complicated the internal forces are.
questions.hint: Distinguish between internal forces (which can exist freely) and external forces (which must sum to zero) for momentum conservation.
distractor_logic: This describes a special consequence in some cases, not the general condition for momentum conservation.
Internal forces are allowed and even expected, such as during a collision; it is the external force that must vanish, not internal forces.
This describes an elastic collision, a separate and stricter condition, not the general condition for momentum conservation.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: A particle is said to be in equilibrium when
options: the vector sum of all forces acting on it is zero
it is completely at rest and never moving
the particle experiences no forces at all
the particle's speed is constant but its direction may change freely
questions.explanation:
A particle is in equilibrium when the vector sum of all the forces acting on it is zero, \( \sum\vec{F}=0 \).

This does not mean no forces act — it means they cancel out.

Equilibrium includes both a particle at rest and one moving with constant velocity in a straight line, but excludes any situation where the direction or speed is changing, since that would require a nonzero net force.
questions.hint: Equilibrium is about the net force, not about whether individual forces exist or whether the particle is moving.
distractor_logic: Equilibrium requires zero net force, which also permits uniform velocity motion, not only being at rest.
Equilibrium requires forces to balance each other, not to be absent altogether.
Constant speed with changing direction implies acceleration, so the net force is not zero; this is not equilibrium.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: The normal force exerted by a surface on an object in contact with it always acts
options: vertically upward, regardless of the surface's orientation
perpendicular to the surface, pointing away from it into the object
along the direction of the object's weight
parallel to the surface, in the direction the object tends to slide
questions.explanation:
The normal force is a contact force that a surface exerts on an object perpendicular to that surface, preventing the object from penetrating it.

On a horizontal surface this happens to be vertical, but on an inclined surface the normal force is perpendicular to the incline itself, not vertical.

Confusing 'normal' with 'vertical' is a common error, especially for problems involving inclined planes.
questions.hint: The word 'normal' in this context means perpendicular to a specific surface, not necessarily vertical.
distractor_logic: This is only true for a horizontal surface; on an inclined surface the normal force is perpendicular to the incline, not vertical.
Weight is always vertical, but the normal force is perpendicular to the surface, which is not always vertical.
This describes friction, not the normal force; friction is parallel to the surface, while the normal force is perpendicular to it.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: For a light (massless), inextensible string passing over a smooth, massless pulley, the tension in the string is
options: greater on the side supporting the heavier weight
zero, since the string itself has no mass
the same throughout the string, on both sides of the pulley
different at each point along the string, decreasing with distance from the pulling force
questions.explanation:
For a massless string, Newton's second law applied to any tiny segment of the string gives zero net force on that segment (since it has zero mass), which forces the tension to be identical at every point along the string.

An ideal (massless, frictionless) pulley only changes the direction of the string's tension, not its magnitude.

So the tension is the same throughout the string, on both sides of the pulley, regardless of the masses attached at either end.
questions.hint: For an ideal massless string over an ideal frictionless, massless pulley, no force is 'lost' anywhere along the string.
distractor_logic: For a massless string and an ideal frictionless, massless pulley, tension is uniform throughout, regardless of what is attached at either end.
A massless string can still transmit a nonzero tension force; masslessness affects only the string's own inertia, not the force it carries.
For an ideal massless string over an ideal frictionless pulley, tension does not vary along its length; this would only occur for a string with mass or a pulley with friction.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: According to Hooke's law, \( F=-kx \), for a spring stretched by a positive displacement \( x \) from its natural length, the spring force
options: acts in the same direction as the displacement, stretching the spring further
has a constant magnitude regardless of how far the spring is stretched
only acts when the spring is compressed, not when it is stretched
acts in the direction opposite to the displacement, pulling the spring back toward its natural length
questions.explanation:
Hooke's law states \( F=-kx \), where \( x \) is the displacement from the spring's natural (unstretched) length.

The negative sign means the force is always directed opposite to the displacement — so when the spring is stretched (positive \( x \)), the force pulls back toward the natural length.

The same restoring behavior occurs when the spring is compressed (negative \( x \)): the force then pushes outward, again back toward the natural length.
questions.hint: The negative sign in \( F=-kx \) is what makes the spring force a restoring force.
distractor_logic: This would make the spring accelerate away from equilibrium indefinitely; the negative sign in Hooke's law specifically ensures the force always opposes the displacement.
Hooke's law says the force magnitude is proportional to the displacement \( x \), not constant; a more stretched spring pulls back harder.
Hooke's law applies to both stretching and compression; the restoring force acts in both cases, just in opposite directions relative to the equilibrium position.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: A 2 kg object hangs at rest from a single vertical string. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the tension in the string?
questions.explanation:
Since the object hangs at rest, it is in equilibrium, so the tension must exactly balance its weight.

The weight is \( mg=2\times10=20 \) N.

Therefore the tension in the string is \( T=20 \) N.
questions.hint: In equilibrium, the tension must balance the full weight of the hanging object.
distractor_logic: Uses the mass value directly as the tension, forgetting to multiply by \( g \).
Divides the mass by \( g \) instead of multiplying mass by \( g \).
Uses only the value of \( g \) as the tension, ignoring the mass entirely.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: A 5 kg block rests on a horizontal table. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the normal force exerted by the table on the block?
questions.explanation:
The block is in vertical equilibrium, so the normal force must balance its weight.

The weight is \( mg=5\times10=50 \) N.

Therefore the normal force is \( N=50 \) N.
questions.hint: For a block resting on a level table with nothing else pressing on it, the normal force must balance the block's full weight.
distractor_logic: Uses the mass value directly as the normal force, forgetting to multiply by \( g \).
Multiplies mass by \( g^2 \) instead of by \( g \), an incorrect use of the acceleration due to gravity.
Incorrectly assumes that because the block is not moving, no forces act on it at all, rather than recognizing that the normal force balances its weight.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: A spring with spring constant \( k=200 \) N/m is stretched by a force of 8 N. What is the extension of the spring?
questions.explanation:
From Hooke's law, \( F=kx \), so \( x=\dfrac{F}{k} \).

Substituting \( F=8 \) N and \( k=200 \) N/m gives \( x=\dfrac{8}{200}=0.04 \) m.
questions.hint: Rearrange Hooke's law, \( F=kx \), to solve for the extension \( x \).
distractor_logic: Multiplies the force by the spring constant instead of dividing force by spring constant.
Divides the spring constant by the force instead of dividing the force by the spring constant.
Incorrectly adds a leftover term to the extension instead of directly computing \( x=F/k \).

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: A block hangs at rest from a single vertical string, with no other objects in contact with it. How many forces act on the block?
options: One — only the tension in the string, since the block is not touching the ground
One — only its weight, since the string is massless and cannot exert a real force
Three — its weight, the tension, and an additional 'hanging force' holding it in place
Two — its weight and the tension in the string
questions.explanation:
The block has exactly two forces on it: its weight, due to gravity, acting downward, and the tension in the string, acting upward.

These two forces are equal in magnitude (since the block is in equilibrium) but they are not a Newton's third-law pair, since both act on the same body (the block) and are of different natures (gravitational vs. tension).

No other forces are present, since nothing else is in contact with the block.
questions.hint: Only count forces that are genuinely acting on the block itself — from gravity, and from any object physically touching it.
distractor_logic: Gravity acts on the block regardless of whether it touches the ground; weight is always present as long as the block has mass.
A massless string can still exert a completely real tension force on the block; masslessness affects only the string's own inertia.
There is no separate 'hanging force' in Newtonian mechanics; equilibrium is achieved solely by the balance between weight and tension.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: Static friction is the force that
options: opposes the tendency of relative motion between two surfaces in contact that are not yet sliding
always equals \( \mu_sN \), regardless of the applied force
acts only once two surfaces are already sliding past each other
accelerates an object in the direction of relative motion
questions.explanation:
Static friction acts between two surfaces that are not sliding relative to each other, opposing any tendency toward relative motion caused by an applied force.

Unlike a fixed force, static friction adjusts itself to exactly match the applied force (up to a maximum limiting value \( f_{s,max}=\mu_sN \)), so that the object remains at rest as long as the applied force does not exceed that maximum.

Once the applied force exceeds this maximum, sliding begins and kinetic friction takes over.
questions.hint: Static friction is self-adjusting — it responds to whatever tendency toward motion exists, up to a maximum limit.
distractor_logic: Static friction is not fixed at this value; it self-adjusts to match the applied force up to this maximum limit.
This describes kinetic friction, not static friction, which acts before sliding begins.
Friction opposes relative motion (or its tendency); it does not accelerate an object in the direction of sliding.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: Once an object is sliding on a surface, the kinetic friction force acting on it is given by
options: \( f_k=\mu_kmg \), always exactly, regardless of the incline or applied force
\( f_k=\mu_kN \), where \( N \) is the normal force and \( \mu_k \) is the coefficient of kinetic friction
\( f_k=\mu_sN \), using the coefficient of static friction, since it is always larger
\( f_k=\mu_kN^2 \), since friction depends on the square of the normal force
questions.explanation:
The kinetic friction force is given by \( f_k=\mu_kN \), where \( N \) is the actual normal force between the surfaces and \( \mu_k \) is the coefficient of kinetic friction for that pair of surfaces.

On a horizontal surface with no other vertical forces, \( N=mg \), so \( f_k=\mu_kmg \) — but this simplification does not hold in general, such as on an incline, where \( N=mg\cos\theta \).
questions.hint: Kinetic friction depends on the actual normal force between the two surfaces, not simply on the object's weight.
distractor_logic: This is only true on a horizontal surface where \( N=mg \); in general \( f_k \) depends on the actual normal force, which can differ from \( mg \) on an incline or when other forces are present.
Kinetic friction uses \( \mu_k \), not \( \mu_s \); typically \( \mu_k<\mu_s \), not larger.
Friction is directly proportional to the normal force, not its square.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: For a given pair of surfaces, how do the coefficient of static friction \( \mu_s \) and the coefficient of kinetic friction \( \mu_k \) typically compare?
options: \( \mu_s \) and \( \mu_k \) are always exactly equal for any pair of surfaces
questions.explanation:
For most pairs of surfaces, the coefficient of static friction \( \mu_s \) is slightly larger than the coefficient of kinetic friction \( \mu_k \).

This matches everyday experience: it typically takes a larger force to get a stationary object to start sliding than it does to keep it sliding once it is already in motion.

This is why the maximum static friction is usually treated as a slightly higher threshold than the kinetic friction that follows once sliding begins.
questions.hint: Think about which requires more effort: getting a heavy object to start moving from rest, or keeping it moving once it's already sliding.
distractor_logic: This reverses the typical relationship; it usually takes more force to start an object sliding than to keep it sliding.
While they can sometimes be close, they are not generally equal; \( \mu_s \) is typically somewhat larger.
There is no fixed universal ratio between the two coefficients; the relationship depends on the specific surfaces involved.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: The angle of repose of a surface is defined as the angle of inclination at which
options: a block placed on the incline accelerates down at exactly \( g \), regardless of friction
the normal force on the block becomes exactly zero
the block's weight becomes equal to the kinetic friction force, once already sliding
a block placed on the incline is on the verge of sliding down under gravity, with static friction at its maximum value
questions.explanation:
The angle of repose is the incline angle at which a block on the verge of sliding is held in place only by the maximum available static friction.

At this critical angle, the component of gravity along the incline exactly equals the maximum static friction force, so \( mg\sin\theta=\mu_sN=\mu_smg\cos\theta \), giving \( \tan\theta=\mu_s \).

For any angle smaller than this, the block remains at rest; for any angle larger, it begins to slide.
questions.hint: The angle of repose marks the threshold between a block staying at rest and just beginning to slide, using the maximum available static friction.
distractor_logic: This describes free fall, not the angle of repose; friction is very much present and relevant at the angle of repose.
The normal force remains positive at the angle of repose (for any incline angle less than \( 90^\circ \)); it does not vanish.
The angle of repose is about the verge of sliding (using the static, not kinetic, friction limit), not about a block already in steady sliding motion.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: The coefficient of static friction between a block and an incline is \( \mu_s=0.75 \). What is the angle of repose, using \( \tan37°=\tfrac34 \)?
questions.explanation:
The angle of repose satisfies \( \tan\theta=\mu_s \).

Since \( \mu_s=0.75=\tfrac34 \), and \( \tan37°=\tfrac34 \), the angle of repose is \( \theta=37° \).
questions.hint: The angle of repose satisfies \( \tan\theta=\mu_s \); match the given coefficient to the correct standard angle.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \tan53°=\tfrac43 \) instead of matching the given \( \mu_s=0.75=\tfrac34 \) to \( \tan37° \).
Reports the numeric value of \( \mu_s \) itself as if it were the angle in degrees, rather than finding the angle whose tangent equals \( \mu_s \).
Assumes \( \tan\theta=1 \) regardless of the actual given value of \( \mu_s \).

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: The friction force between two surfaces in contact always acts
options: perpendicular to the surfaces, like the normal force
parallel to the surfaces, opposing relative sliding or its tendency
vertically, regardless of the orientation of the surfaces
in the same direction as the applied force, adding to it
questions.explanation:
Friction is a contact force that acts parallel to the surfaces in contact (within the plane of contact), opposing the relative sliding of the surfaces or the tendency toward such sliding.

This is different from the normal force, which acts perpendicular to the surfaces.

Friction's direction is determined by the direction of actual or impending relative motion, not by any fixed direction like vertical.
questions.hint: Friction always lies within the plane of contact between the two surfaces, opposing sliding.
distractor_logic: Perpendicular to the surface describes the normal force, not friction.
Friction's direction depends on the surfaces' orientation and the direction of relative motion (or its tendency), not fixed vertically.
Friction opposes relative motion (or its tendency), so it acts against, not with, the applied force's tendency to cause sliding.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: A block resting on a horizontal surface has a normal force of 40 N acting on it, and the coefficient of static friction between the block and surface is \( \mu_s=0.4 \). What is the maximum possible static friction force?
questions.explanation:
The maximum static friction force is given by \( f_{s,max}=\mu_sN \).

Substituting \( \mu_s=0.4 \) and \( N=40 \) N gives \( f_{s,max}=0.4\times40=16 \) N.
questions.hint: The maximum static friction force is the coefficient of static friction multiplied by the normal force.
distractor_logic: Divides the normal force by the coefficient of friction instead of multiplying.
Adds the normal force and the coefficient of friction instead of multiplying them.
Uses a misplaced decimal, effectively dividing the correct answer by 10.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: A 20 N horizontal force is applied to a block resting on a rough floor, but the block does not move. The maximum possible static friction force on this block is 30 N. What is the actual magnitude of the friction force acting on the block?
questions.explanation:
Since the block remains at rest, it is in equilibrium, so the actual friction force must exactly balance the applied horizontal force.

Friction is self-adjusting: it takes on whatever value is needed to prevent sliding, up to its maximum limit of 30 N.

Since the applied force of 20 N is less than this maximum, the actual friction force is simply 20 N — not the maximum value of 30 N.
questions.hint: If the block is not moving, the actual friction force must exactly balance the applied force — it need not be at its maximum possible value.
distractor_logic: This assumes friction is always at its maximum possible value, rather than recognizing that static friction self-adjusts to exactly match the applied force as long as the object remains at rest.
Computes the difference between the maximum friction and the applied force, rather than recognizing that friction itself simply equals the applied force here.
Adds the applied force and the maximum friction value instead of recognizing that friction only matches the applied force needed to keep the block at rest.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: Centripetal force is best described as
options: the name given to whichever net real force (such as tension, gravity, friction, or a normal force component) provides the center-directed acceleration for circular motion
an additional force that must be added to the free-body diagram alongside the real forces acting on the object
a force that always points away from the center of the circular path
a force that exists only for objects moving in a perfect circle at constant speed
questions.explanation:
Centripetal force does not name a new, distinct type of force; it is simply the name given to whichever net real force — tension in a string, gravity, friction, a component of the normal force, or some combination — happens to be directed toward the center and supplies the acceleration \( a_c=v^2/r \) needed for circular motion.

Because of this, centripetal force should never be added as an extra arrow on a free-body diagram alongside the forces that are already providing it — doing so double-counts the same physical force.

Its direction is always toward the center of the circular path, at any given instant.
questions.hint: Centripetal force is not a separate, additional force — it's a label for the role that some already-existing real force is playing.
distractor_logic: This double-counts the same physical force; centripetal force is not a separate force to add, it IS whichever real force already provides the center-directed acceleration.
Centripetal force points toward the center, not away from it; an outward-pointing effect would instead describe the fictitious centrifugal effect.

Centripetal force is simply whatever net force produces center-directed acceleration; it is relevant whenever there is a center-directed component of acceleration, not only in uniform circular motion.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: An object moves in a circle of radius \( r \) with constant speed \( v \). What is the magnitude of its centripetal acceleration?
questions.explanation:
For an object moving in a circle of radius \( r \) with constant speed \( v \), the centripetal acceleration is \( a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r} \), directed toward the center of the circle at every instant.

This acceleration exists even though the speed is constant, because the direction of the velocity is continuously changing.
questions.hint: Recall the standard formula for centripetal acceleration in terms of speed and radius.
distractor_logic: This omits the correct squaring of the speed; centripetal acceleration depends on \( v^2 \), not \( v \) alone.
This incorrectly multiplies speed and radius rather than using the correct ratio \( v^2/r \).
This inverts the correct relationship, placing the radius in the numerator (squared) and speed in the denominator.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: For an object undergoing uniform circular motion, the centripetal force on it points
options: in the same direction as the object's velocity at every instant
away from the center of the circular path
toward the center of the circular path, at every instant
in a fixed direction in space, the same at every point on the circle
questions.explanation:
By definition, centripetal force is always directed toward the center of the circular path, regardless of where the object currently is on that path.

Since the object's position is constantly changing as it moves around the circle, the actual direction of the centripetal force in space is constantly changing too — always pointing from the object's current location toward the center.

This is fundamentally different from the object's velocity, which is always tangent to the circle, perpendicular to the centripetal force.
questions.hint: The word 'centripetal' literally means 'center-seeking' — think about what direction that implies at every point on the circle.
distractor_logic: The velocity is tangent to the circle, while the centripetal force is perpendicular to the velocity, directed toward the center — these are two different directions.
This describes the outward direction, opposite to the actual direction of the centripetal force.
The centripetal force always points from the object's current position toward the center, so its direction in space continuously changes as the object moves around the circle.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: A car moves in a circle of radius 50 m at a constant speed of 10 m/s. What is the magnitude of its centripetal acceleration?
questions.explanation: The centripetal acceleration is \( a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r}=\dfrac{10^2}{50}=\dfrac{100}{50}=2 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: Square the speed before dividing by the radius.
distractor_logic: Divides speed by radius without squaring the speed first.
Multiplies the speed squared by the radius instead of dividing by it.
Divides the radius by the speed instead of dividing the speed squared by the radius.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: A 2 kg object moves in a circle of radius 4 m at a constant speed of 6 m/s. What is the magnitude of the centripetal force acting on it?
questions.explanation:
The centripetal acceleration is \( a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r}=\dfrac{6^2}{4}=\dfrac{36}{4}=9 \) m/s\(^2\).

The centripetal force is \( F_c=ma_c=2\times9=18 \) N.
questions.hint: First find the centripetal acceleration \( v^2/r \), then multiply by the mass to get the centripetal force.
distractor_logic: Divides speed squared by radius correctly to get acceleration but forgets to multiply by the mass to get force.
Uses the speed, not speed squared, multiplied by mass and radius in an incorrect combination.
Multiplies the speed squared by both the mass and the radius, instead of dividing by the radius.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: Roads are banked (built with the outer edge raised higher than the inner edge) at curves primarily in order to
options: eliminate the need for a centripetal force altogether while turning
allow a component of the normal force to help supply the centripetal force needed for the turn, reducing reliance on friction
increase the friction between the tires and the road surface
make the road surface more visually distinct for drivers approaching a curve
questions.explanation:
On a banked road, the normal force is no longer purely vertical; it has a horizontal component directed toward the center of the curve.

This horizontal component of the normal force helps supply the centripetal force needed for the vehicle to turn, reducing how much the vehicle has to rely on friction alone.

At an appropriately banked angle for a given speed, a vehicle can even take the turn safely with zero friction required.
questions.hint: Think about how tilting the road changes the direction of the normal force acting on a vehicle.
distractor_logic: Circular motion always requires a net center-directed force; banking does not eliminate this need, it simply supplies part of it more effectively using the normal force.
Banking changes the direction of the normal force so that it contributes to the centripetal force; it does not primarily work by increasing the friction coefficient itself.
Banking is a matter of vehicle dynamics and safety, providing part of the required centripetal force, not merely a visual or aesthetic design choice.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: For a vehicle taking a frictionless banked curve of radius \( r \) at the optimum (design) speed, banked at angle \( \theta \), which formula correctly relates the optimum speed \( v \) to \( r \), \( g \), and \( \theta \)?
questions.explanation:
For a frictionless banked curve, only the normal force acts (aside from gravity), and it must supply both vertical support and the horizontal centripetal force.

Balancing vertical and horizontal components gives \( N\cos\theta=mg \) and \( N\sin\theta=\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \).

Dividing these two equations eliminates \( N \) and \( m \), giving \( \tan\theta=\dfrac{v^2}{rg} \), so \( v=\sqrt{rg\tan\theta} \).
questions.hint: Resolve the normal force into horizontal and vertical components, and divide the horizontal force equation by the vertical one to eliminate the normal force and find \( v \).
distractor_logic: This uses \( \sin\theta \) alone instead of the correct combination \( \tan\theta \), which comes from dividing the horizontal and vertical force-balance equations.
This omits the square root; the correct relationship involves the square root of \( rg\tan\theta \), not that quantity directly.
This inverts \( \tan\theta \), placing it in the denominator instead of the numerator.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: A car goes around a flat (unbanked), horizontal curve. What provides the centripetal force needed to keep the car on the curved path?
options: The car's own engine power, pushing the car forward along its direction of travel
The normal force from the road, which on a flat road always has a horizontal component toward the center
The car's weight, since gravity always pulls objects toward the center of any circular path they follow
Friction between the tires and the road, directed toward the center of the curve
questions.explanation:
On a flat, unbanked horizontal curve, the normal force is purely vertical (balancing the car's weight) and gravity is also purely vertical, so neither can supply a horizontal centripetal force.

The only force available to provide the necessary center-directed force is friction between the tires and the road surface, directed horizontally toward the center of the curve.

If the required centripetal force exceeds the maximum available friction, the car cannot maintain the curved path and skids outward.
questions.hint: On a flat, horizontal curve, which of the forces present actually has a component pointing horizontally, toward the center of the curve?
distractor_logic: Engine power provides forward thrust along the direction of motion, which is tangent to the curve, not toward the center; it cannot supply a center-directed force.
On a genuinely flat (horizontal) road, the normal force is purely vertical and has no horizontal component at all; only a banked road can provide a horizontal component of the normal force.

Gravity pulls straight down, which is not necessarily toward the center of a horizontal curve; on a flat curve, gravity is balanced by the vertical normal force and plays no role in the horizontal centripetal force.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: Two horizontal forces act on a 2 kg block: 10 N to the east and 4 N to the west. What is the block's acceleration?
questions.explanation:
Taking east as positive, the net force is \( F_{net}=10-4=6 \) N (east).

Applying Newton's second law, \( a=\dfrac{F_{net}}{m}=\dfrac{6}{2}=3 \) m/s\(^2\).

Since \( F_{net} \) is positive, the acceleration is directed east.
questions.hint: First combine the two forces into a single net force, keeping track of direction, then apply \( a=F_{net}/m \).
distractor_logic: Adds the two forces instead of finding their vector difference before dividing by mass.
Gets the correct magnitude but reverses the subtraction order, flipping the direction of the net force.
Divides the net force by an incorrect effective mass rather than the block's actual 2 kg mass.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A constant force of 8 N acts on a body for 5 s. What is the magnitude of the change in the body's momentum?
questions.explanation:
By the impulse-momentum theorem, \( \Delta p=F\times\Delta t \) for a constant force.

Substituting \( F=8 \) N and \( \Delta t=5 \) s gives \( \Delta p=8\times5=40 \) kg m/s.
questions.hint: Impulse equals force multiplied by the time for which it acts, and impulse is exactly the change in momentum.
distractor_logic: Divides force by time instead of multiplying them.
Adds force and time instead of multiplying them.
Divides time by force instead of multiplying force by time.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A car of mass 1000 kg moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest uniformly in 4 s by the brakes. What is the magnitude of the average braking force?
questions.explanation:
The deceleration is \( a=\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{20-0}{4}=5 \) m/s\(^2\).

By Newton's second law, the magnitude of the braking force is \( F=ma=1000\times5=5000 \) N.
questions.hint: First find the deceleration from the given initial velocity and time, then apply Newton's second law with the actual mass.
distractor_logic: Uses the initial velocity directly in place of the deceleration, without dividing by the time taken.
Combines mass, velocity and time in an inverted ratio instead of computing \( a=\Delta v/\Delta t \) first and then \( F=ma \).
Finds the correct deceleration of 5 m/s\(^2\) but then multiplies by an incorrect mass of 800 kg instead of the given 1000 kg.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A 2 kg block, initially at rest, is pushed by a constant horizontal force of 6 N on a frictionless surface. How far does it travel in the first 3 s?
questions.explanation:
The acceleration is \( a=\dfrac{F}{m}=\dfrac{6}{2}=3 \) m/s\(^2\).

Starting from rest, the distance covered in time \( t \) is \( s=\dfrac12at^2=\dfrac12\times3\times3^2=13.5 \) m.
questions.hint: Find the acceleration from Newton's second law first, then use the kinematic equation for distance starting from rest.
distractor_logic: Computes distance as \( at \) instead of using \( s=\tfrac12at^2 \) for motion starting from rest.
Uses \( s=at^2 \), omitting the factor of \( \tfrac12 \).
Finds the correct acceleration of 3 m/s\(^2\) but mistakenly uses \( t=6 \) s in the formula instead of the given 3 s.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: Two blocks of masses 3 kg and 2 kg are placed in contact on a frictionless floor, with the 3 kg block in front. A horizontal force of 20 N is applied to the rear (2 kg) block, pushing both blocks together. What is the magnitude of the contact force that the rear block exerts on the front block?
questions.explanation:
Treating both blocks as one system of total mass 5 kg, the common acceleration is \( a=\dfrac{F}{m_{total}}=\dfrac{20}{5}=4 \) m/s\(^2\).

For the front 3 kg block alone, the only horizontal force is the contact force \( N \) from the rear block, so \( N=m_{front}\,a=3\times4=12 \) N.
questions.hint: First find the common acceleration of the whole system, then apply Newton's second law to just the front block, on which only the contact force acts horizontally.
distractor_logic: Assumes the entire applied force is transmitted to the front block, ignoring that part of it also accelerates the rear block.
Uses the contact force to accelerate only the rear block's own 2 kg mass rather than the front 3 kg block it is pushing.
Splits the applied force equally between the two blocks by count rather than in proportion to their masses.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: Object A has mass 2 kg and speed 6 m/s. Object B has mass 3 kg and speed 5 m/s. Which object has greater momentum, and by how much?
questions.explanation:
Momentum of A: \( p_A=2\times6=12 \) kg m/s.

Momentum of B: \( p_B=3\times5=15 \) kg m/s.

Since \( p_B>p_A \), object B has greater momentum, exceeding A's by \( 15-12=3 \) kg m/s.
questions.hint: Compute \( p=mv \) separately for each object before comparing.
distractor_logic: Correctly computes the 3 kg m/s difference but assigns it to the wrong object.
Mis-multiplies or mis-subtracts the momentum values rather than directly comparing \( p=mv \) for each object.
Incorrectly assumes momentum depends only on mass or only on speed rather than on their product.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A velocity-time graph for a 4 kg object is a straight line rising from 2 m/s to 14 m/s over 3 s. What is the magnitude of the constant net force acting on the object?
questions.explanation:
The slope of the v-t graph gives the acceleration: \( a=\dfrac{14-2}{3}=4 \) m/s\(^2\).

By Newton's second law, the net force is \( F=ma=4\times4=16 \) N.
questions.hint: The slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration; then apply \( F=ma \).
distractor_logic: Uses the total change in velocity directly as the acceleration, without dividing by the 3 s time interval.
Multiplies the final velocity by the mass instead of first finding the acceleration from the graph's slope.
Divides the acceleration by the mass instead of multiplying acceleration by mass.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A force-time graph for a body shows a constant force of 10 N acting from \( t=0 \) to \( t=6 \) s. What impulse does the body receive over this interval?
questions.explanation:
Impulse is the area under the force-time graph.

Since the force is constant at 10 N over the 6 s interval, the graph is a rectangle of area \( 10\times6=60 \) N s.

This equals the change in the body's momentum, \( \Delta p=60 \) kg m/s (numerically the same, since 1 N s = 1 kg m/s).
questions.hint: Impulse equals the area under a force-time graph; for a constant force this area is a rectangle.
distractor_logic: Adds the force and the time interval instead of finding the area under the force-time graph.
Divides the force by the time instead of computing force times time.
Treats the rectangular force-time graph as if it were a triangle, unnecessarily halving the area.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley and they stick together. What is their common velocity just after the collision?
options: 3 m/s (in the direction of the moving trolley's initial motion)
questions.explanation:
Since no external horizontal force acts during the brief collision, momentum is conserved: \( m_1v_1+m_2v_2=(m_1+m_2)v \).

Substituting, \( 3\times4+1\times0=(3+1)v \), giving \( 12=4v \).

So \( v=3 \) m/s, in the direction the 3 kg trolley was originally moving.
questions.hint: Momentum is conserved in the collision; use the total momentum before impact and the combined mass afterward.
distractor_logic: Assumes the moving trolley's velocity is unaffected by the collision, ignoring the added mass of the stationary trolley.
Divides the initial momentum by an incorrect total mass instead of the correct combined mass of 4 kg.
Reports the total momentum value (12 kg m/s) directly as if it were the velocity, forgetting to divide by the total mass.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: A gun of mass 4 kg, initially at rest, fires a 0.02 kg bullet with a forward speed of 400 m/s. What is the recoil speed of the gun?
questions.explanation:
Before firing, total momentum is zero. The bullet's momentum after firing is \( p_{bullet}=0.02\times400=8 \) kg m/s (forward).

By conservation of momentum, the gun must acquire equal and opposite momentum: \( p_{gun}=8 \) kg m/s (backward).

The gun's recoil speed is \( v_{gun}=\dfrac{p_{gun}}{m_{gun}}=\dfrac{8}{4}=2 \) m/s.
questions.hint: The total momentum of the (gun+bullet) system stays zero, so the gun's momentum must equal the bullet's momentum in magnitude.
distractor_logic: Uses the bullet's momentum value directly as the gun's recoil speed, without dividing by the gun's mass.
Divides the gun's mass by the bullet's momentum instead of dividing the bullet's momentum by the gun's mass.
Uses the bullet's mass multiplied by an incorrect factor instead of equating the gun's and bullet's momenta directly.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: Two carts at rest, of masses 2 kg and 6 kg, are pushed apart by a spring between them (no external force). If the 2 kg cart moves off at 9 m/s, what is the speed of the 6 kg cart?
options: 3 m/s, in the opposite direction to the 2 kg cart
questions.explanation:
Since the total momentum of the (2 kg + 6 kg) system remains zero, \( m_1v_1=m_2v_2 \) in magnitude, with the carts moving in opposite directions.

The 2 kg cart's momentum is \( 2\times9=18 \) kg m/s.

So the 6 kg cart's speed is \( v_2=\dfrac{18}{6}=3 \) m/s, directed opposite to the 2 kg cart.
questions.hint: Total momentum starts and stays at zero; equate the magnitudes of the two carts' momenta, not their speeds.
distractor_logic: Assumes both carts must move at the same speed regardless of their different masses.
Multiplies rather than divides when relating the two carts' momenta.
Combines the masses and speed in an incorrect ratio instead of directly equating the two carts' momenta.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: A block sliding on a rough horizontal floor collides with a second, stationary block and they move off together. Is the total momentum of the two-block system conserved during this brief collision?
options: No, never — because friction, an external force, is always acting on the system
Yes, always exactly — friction has no effect on momentum whatsoever
No, because the two blocks now have different masses acting as one, so momentum has no meaning for combined bodies
Approximately yes — the collision force is far larger than friction over the very short collision time, so friction's impulse is negligible
questions.explanation:
Friction is indeed an external force on the two-block system, so momentum is not exactly conserved for the system as a whole over any extended time.

However, during the collision itself, the collision (internal) force is extremely large and acts only for a very short time, while friction is comparatively small.

So the impulse due to friction during the brief collision is negligible, and momentum conservation is used as an excellent working approximation for the instant of collision — even though the same is not true if friction acts over a longer subsequent time.
questions.hint: Compare the very short duration of the collision itself to the relatively small friction force acting throughout — which impulse dominates?
distractor_logic: This overstates friction's effect; its impulse over the extremely brief collision time is negligible compared to the large internal collision force, making momentum conservation an excellent approximation.
This incorrectly claims friction never affects momentum at all, ignoring that over a longer time it certainly does change the system's momentum.
Momentum conservation applies perfectly well to combined or composite bodies; combining masses does not invalidate momentum at all.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: A person of mass 60 kg standing at rest on a stationary boat of mass 140 kg jumps off horizontally, leaving the boat moving at 3 m/s in the opposite direction to the person. What is the person's speed just after jumping?
questions.explanation:
Before jumping, the (person + boat) system is at rest, so total momentum is zero.

The boat's momentum after the jump is \( p_{boat}=140\times3=420 \) kg m/s.

By conservation of momentum, the person's momentum must be equal and opposite: \( p_{person}=420 \) kg m/s, so \( v_{person}=\dfrac{420}{60}=7 \) m/s.
questions.hint: The system starts with zero total momentum, so the person's momentum must exactly balance the boat's momentum in magnitude.
distractor_logic: Assumes the person and boat must have the same speed, ignoring their different masses.
Applies an unrelated mass-fraction calculation instead of directly equating the person's and boat's momenta.
Divides the boat's momentum by the combined mass of person and boat (200 kg) rather than by the person's mass alone.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: Two blocks are connected by a light, inextensible string, and block A pulls on the string with a tension force. What is the genuine Newton's third-law reaction to this tension force that block A exerts on the string?
options: The tension force the string exerts on block B at its other end
The tension force the string exerts back on block A
The force block B exerts on block A through the string
questions.explanation:
Block A exerts a tension force on the string (pulling it).

By Newton's third law, the string exerts an equal and opposite tension force back on block A.

The tension at the string's other end, acting on block B, is equal in magnitude only because the string is light (massless) and inextensible — it is a separate force in its own right, not the third-law partner of the force block A exerts on the string.
questions.hint: The reaction to a force that block A exerts on the string must be a force the string exerts back on block A — the same two objects, force reversed.
distractor_logic: This is a different force acting on a different (third) body — block B — and is equal only because the string is light and inextensible, not because it is a third-law pair to the force on A.
This pairs a tension force with a gravitational force on the same body; different force types can never be a third-law pair.
This conflates the string's own tension with a direct force between the two blocks; the true third-law pair to A's pull on the string is the string's pull back on A.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on with a 3 kg ball moving at 2 m/s in the opposite direction. After the collision, the 2 kg ball is at rest. What is the velocity of the 3 kg ball after the collision?
options: 2 m/s, in the direction the 3 kg ball was originally moving
1.2 m/s, in the direction the 2 kg ball was originally moving
2 m/s, in the direction the 2 kg ball was originally moving
4 m/s, in the direction the 2 kg ball was originally moving
questions.explanation:
Taking the 2 kg ball's initial direction as positive, the total momentum before collision is \( p_i=2\times6+3\times(-2)=12-6=6 \) kg m/s.

After the collision, momentum is still conserved: \( p_f=2\times0+3\times v_2=6 \) kg m/s.

Solving, \( v_2=\dfrac{6}{3}=2 \) m/s, in the direction the 2 kg ball was originally moving.
questions.hint: Set a consistent positive direction, write the total momentum before and after the collision, and solve for the unknown final velocity of the 3 kg ball.
distractor_logic: Gets the correct magnitude but assigns the wrong direction, mishandling the sign convention for the two balls' initial velocities.
Divides the total system momentum (6 kg m/s) by the combined mass of both balls (5 kg), as though both balls end up moving together, instead of solving for the 3 kg ball's velocity alone.
Omits the 3 kg ball's own initial momentum from the total, using only the 2 kg ball's initial momentum (12 kg m/s) as if it were the whole system's total.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: During a collision between a heavy truck and a light car, how do the magnitudes of the force the truck exerts on the car and the force the car exerts on the truck compare, at each instant of the collision?
options: The truck exerts a much larger force on the car than the car exerts on the truck, because the truck is heavier
The forces are equal only at the single instant of maximum contact, and unequal at all other times
The forces are equal in magnitude only if the collision is perfectly elastic
They are exactly equal in magnitude at every instant, by Newton's third law
questions.explanation:
By Newton's third law, the force the truck exerts on the car and the force the car exerts on the truck are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction at every instant of the collision, regardless of the vehicles' masses.

What differs is the resulting acceleration of each vehicle: since \( a=F/m \), the lighter car experiences a much larger acceleration than the heavier truck for the same force magnitude.

This is often misunderstood as the truck 'hitting harder,' but the forces themselves are always equal — only the effects differ.
questions.hint: Newton's third law does not depend on the relative masses of the two objects — only the resulting accelerations depend on mass.
distractor_logic: Mass has no bearing on the magnitude of the third-law force pair; only the resulting accelerations differ because the masses differ, not the forces themselves.
Newton's third law holds at every instant of the interaction, not just at one special moment.
