Newton's third law holds regardless of whether the collision is elastic or inelastic; it is unrelated to whether kinetic energy is conserved.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: A 10 kg object hangs in equilibrium, held by two strings attached to the ceiling at the same point where the object hangs. One string makes \( 37° \) with the horizontal ceiling and the other makes \( 53° \) with the ceiling, with the two strings perpendicular to each other. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \), what is the tension in the string making \( 37° \) with the ceiling?
questions.explanation:
With the strings perpendicular to each other and making \( 37° \) and \( 53° \) with the horizontal ceiling, resolving forces at the hanging point gives \( T_{37}=mg\sin37° \) and \( T_{53}=mg\cos37° \) (equivalently \( mg\sin53° \)).

The weight is \( mg=10\times10=100 \) N.

So the tension in the \( 37° \) string is \( T_{37}=100\times\tfrac35=60 \) N.
questions.hint: Resolve forces along the horizontal and vertical directions at the point where the strings meet, using the fact that the two strings are perpendicular to each other.
distractor_logic: Computes the tension in the other string, the one at \( 53° \), instead of the one at \( 37° \) asked for.
Assumes the entire weight is carried by a single string, ignoring that the load is shared between the two strings at an angle.
Multiplies the weight by an incorrect trigonometric ratio instead of using the correct value \( \tfrac35 \) for \( \sin37° \).

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: A 4 kg block rests on a frictionless incline making \( 37° \) with the horizontal, held in place by a string parallel to the incline surface attached to the top. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \), what is the normal force exerted by the incline on the block?
questions.explanation:
Resolving the weight \( mg=4\times10=40 \) N into components parallel and perpendicular to the incline, the perpendicular component is \( mg\cos37° \) and is balanced by the normal force.

So \( N=mg\cos37°=40\times\tfrac45=32 \) N.

(The parallel component, \( mg\sin37°=40\times\tfrac35=24 \) N, is instead balanced by the tension in the string.)
questions.hint: Only the component of the block's weight perpendicular to the incline contributes to the normal force; the component along the incline is balanced by the string.
distractor_logic: Uses the block's full weight as the normal force, ignoring that only the component perpendicular to the incline contributes to the normal force.
Uses \( \sin37° \) instead of \( \cos37° \), mixing up which weight component is perpendicular to the incline.
Computes the tension in the string (the component of weight along the incline, \( mg\sin37° \)) instead of the normal force.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: Two blocks of mass 3 kg and 5 kg are connected by a light, inextensible string over a smooth, massless pulley, hanging freely on either side (an Atwood machine). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the magnitude of the acceleration of the system?
questions.explanation:
For an Atwood machine, the acceleration is \( a=\dfrac{(m_2-m_1)g}{m_1+m_2} \), where \( m_2>m_1 \).

Substituting \( m_1=3 \) kg, \( m_2=5 \) kg, and \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\): \( a=\dfrac{(5-3)\times10}{3+5}=\dfrac{20}{8}=2.5 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: For an Atwood machine, the acceleration equals the net weight difference divided by the total mass of both blocks, since both blocks share the same magnitude of acceleration through the inextensible string.
distractor_logic: Uses \( g \) directly as the acceleration, ignoring that both masses share the load and partly balance each other.
Uses only the difference in mass (2 kg) with \( g \) but forgets to divide by the total mass of the system (8 kg).
Divides the mass difference by twice the correct total mass, an incorrect combination of the two masses.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: In the same Atwood machine (3 kg and 5 kg blocks connected over a smooth, massless pulley, \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\)), what is the tension in the string?
questions.explanation:
Applying Newton's second law to the lighter (3 kg) block, which accelerates upward: \( T-m_1g=m_1a \), so \( T=m_1(g+a)=3\times(10+2.5)=37.5 \) N.

Checking with the heavier (5 kg) block, which accelerates downward: \( m_2g-T=m_2a \), so \( T=m_2(g-a)=5\times(10-2.5)=37.5 \) N — consistent, as expected since the string has a single tension throughout.
questions.hint: Apply Newton's second law to just one of the two blocks, using the acceleration you already found, to solve for the tension.
distractor_logic: Adds the weights of both blocks (\( m_1g+m_2g \)) instead of properly applying Newton's second law to the accelerating system.
Uses only the lighter block's weight (\( m_1g \)) as the tension, ignoring that the system is accelerating rather than in equilibrium.
Uses only the heavier block's weight (\( m_2g \)) as the tension, similarly ignoring the system's acceleration.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: A vertical spring stretches by 5 cm when a 2 kg mass is hung from it and allowed to come to rest. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the spring constant?
questions.explanation:
The weight supported by the spring is \( F=mg=2\times10=20 \) N.

The extension is \( x=5\text{ cm}=0.05 \) m.

By Hooke's law, \( k=\dfrac{F}{x}=\dfrac{20}{0.05}=400 \) N/m.
questions.hint: Convert the extension to metres, find the weight supported, and use Hooke's law \( k=F/x \).
distractor_logic: Reports the extension itself (in different units) rather than computing the spring constant from \( k=F/x \).
Uses the mass value directly divided by the extension (\( m/x \)) instead of the weight (\( mg/x \)).
Divides \( g \) by the extension instead of dividing the full weight \( mg \) by the extension.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: Two blocks of mass 2 kg and 4 kg are connected by a light string and lie on a frictionless floor, with the 4 kg block in front. A horizontal force of 18 N is applied to the rear (2 kg) block, pulling both blocks via the string. What is the tension in the string connecting them?
questions.explanation:
Treating both blocks as one system of total mass 6 kg, the common acceleration is \( a=\dfrac{F}{m_{total}}=\dfrac{18}{6}=3 \) m/s\(^2\).

For the front 4 kg block alone, the only horizontal force is the tension \( T \) from the string, so \( T=m_{front}\,a=4\times3=12 \) N.
questions.hint: First find the common acceleration of the whole system, then apply Newton's second law to just the front block, on which only the tension acts horizontally.
distractor_logic: Assumes the entire applied force is transmitted through the string to the front block, ignoring that part of the force also accelerates the rear block itself.
Uses the tension to accelerate only the rear block's own mass instead of the front block that the string is pulling.
Splits the applied force equally between the two blocks by count rather than in proportion to their masses.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: A 2 kg block on a frictionless horizontal table is connected by a light string, over a smooth pulley at the table's edge, to a 3 kg block hanging freely. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the magnitude of the acceleration of the system?
questions.explanation:
Since only the hanging 3 kg block's weight drives the motion (the table block has no gravity component along the direction of motion, and the tension is internal to the two-block system), \( a=\dfrac{m_2g}{m_1+m_2} \), where \( m_2 \) is the hanging mass.

Substituting \( m_1=2 \) kg, \( m_2=3 \) kg: \( a=\dfrac{3\times10}{2+3}=\dfrac{30}{5}=6 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: Treat both blocks as one system being driven by only the hanging block's weight, since the string tension is internal to that system.
distractor_logic: Uses \( g \) directly, ignoring that the table block's inertia also resists the acceleration of the whole system.
Divides the hanging block's weight by only its own mass (3 kg), rather than by the total mass of both blocks (5 kg).
Divides the hanging block's weight by an incorrect combination such as twice the total mass, instead of the total mass of both blocks.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: For the same table-and-pulley system (2 kg block on a frictionless table, connected to a 3 kg hanging block, \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\)), what is the tension in the string?
questions.explanation:
For the 2 kg block on the table, the tension is the only horizontal force, so \( T=m_1a=2\times6=12 \) N.

Checking with the hanging 3 kg block: \( m_2g-T=m_2a \), so \( T=m_2(g-a)=3\times(10-6)=12 \) N — consistent.
questions.hint: Apply Newton's second law to just the block on the table, for which the only horizontal force is the tension, using the acceleration you already found.
distractor_logic: Uses the full weight of the hanging block as the tension, as if the system were in equilibrium rather than accelerating.
Uses the table block's weight (\( m_1g \), which plays no role in the horizontal tension) instead of \( m_1a \).
Uses the hanging block's mass multiplied by an incorrect acceleration value rather than the correctly found 6 m/s\(^2\).

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: A 5 kg block rests on a horizontal floor with \( \mu_s=0.5 \) and \( \mu_k=0.4 \). A horizontal force of 30 N is applied. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), does the block move, and if so, what is its acceleration?
options: Yes, it moves; acceleration is 2 m/s\(^2\)
No, it stays at rest, since friction can rise to match any applied force
Yes, it moves; acceleration is 6 m/s\(^2\)
Yes, it moves; acceleration is 1 m/s\(^2\)
questions.explanation:
The maximum static friction is \( f_{s,max}=\mu_sN=0.5\times(5\times10)=25 \) N.

Since the applied force of 30 N exceeds this maximum, the block begins to slide, and kinetic friction now acts: \( f_k=\mu_kN=0.4\times50=20 \) N.

The net force is \( 30-20=10 \) N, so the acceleration is \( a=\dfrac{10}{5}=2 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: First check whether the applied force exceeds the maximum static friction; if it does, the block slides, and you should then use the kinetic friction (not the static value) to find the net force.
distractor_logic: Friction cannot exceed its maximum value \( f_{s,max}=\mu_sN=25 \) N; since the applied force of 30 N exceeds this, the block must begin to slide.
Uses the full applied force (30 N) divided by mass, ignoring that kinetic friction continues to oppose the motion once sliding begins.
Uses the maximum static friction (25 N) instead of the kinetic friction (20 N) to find the net force once the block is already sliding.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: A 10 kg block rests on a horizontal floor with \( \mu_s=0.6 \). A horizontal force of 40 N is applied, and the block does not move. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the actual magnitude of the friction force acting on the block?
questions.explanation:
The maximum possible static friction is \( f_{s,max}=\mu_sN=0.6\times(10\times10)=60 \) N.

Since the applied force of 40 N is less than this maximum, the block remains at rest, and the actual friction force must exactly balance the applied force.

So the friction force is 40 N — not the maximum value of 60 N.
questions.hint: Since the block stays at rest, friction is not at its maximum — it simply matches whatever applied force is needed for equilibrium.
distractor_logic: Uses the maximum possible static friction value instead of recognizing that friction only matches the actual applied force needed to prevent sliding.
Uses the block's full weight instead of the applied horizontal force to determine the friction.
Computes the difference between the maximum static friction and the applied force instead of recognizing friction simply equals the applied force here.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: A block is placed on an incline where the coefficient of static friction is \( \mu_s=\tfrac43 \). What is the angle of repose, using \( \tan53°=\tfrac43 \)?
questions.explanation:
The angle of repose satisfies \( \tan\theta=\mu_s \).

Since \( \mu_s=\tfrac43 \) and \( \tan53°=\tfrac43 \), the angle of repose is \( \theta=53° \).
questions.hint: Match the given coefficient of friction to the standard angle whose tangent equals that value.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \tan37°=\tfrac34 \), the reciprocal of the correct ratio, instead of matching \( \mu_s=\tfrac43 \) to \( \tan53° \).
Reports the numeric value of \( \mu_s \) directly as if it were the angle in degrees.
Assumes \( \tan\theta=1 \) regardless of the actual given value of \( \mu_s \).

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: A 4 kg block is placed on an incline of \( 53° \) with the horizontal, where \( \mu_s=0.5 \) and \( \mu_k=0.4 \). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin53°=\tfrac45 \), \( \cos53°=\tfrac35 \), does the block slide down, and if so, what is its acceleration down the incline?
options: No, it stays at rest, since the incline surface always provides enough friction to prevent sliding
Yes, it slides; acceleration is 8 m/s\(^2\) down the incline
Yes, it slides; acceleration is 5 m/s\(^2\) down the incline
Yes, it slides; acceleration is 5.6 m/s\(^2\) down the incline
questions.explanation:
The component of gravity along the incline is \( mg\sin53°=4\times10\times\tfrac45=32 \) N, and the normal force is \( N=mg\cos53°=4\times10\times\tfrac35=24 \) N.

The maximum static friction is \( f_{s,max}=\mu_sN=0.5\times24=12 \) N, which is far less than the 32 N driving force, so the block slides.

Once sliding, kinetic friction is \( f_k=\mu_kN=0.4\times24=9.6 \) N, giving a net force of \( 32-9.6=22.4 \) N and an acceleration of \( a=\dfrac{22.4}{4}=5.6 \) m/s\(^2\) down the incline.
questions.hint: First compare the component of gravity along the incline to the maximum static friction to decide if the block slides; if it does, switch to using the kinetic friction coefficient for the net force.
distractor_logic: Friction has a maximum limit \( \mu_sN \); here the driving force along the incline (32 N) far exceeds the maximum static friction (12 N), so the block cannot stay at rest.
Ignores kinetic friction entirely once sliding begins, using only \( g\sin53° \) as the acceleration.
Uses the maximum static friction (12 N) instead of the kinetic friction (9.6 N) to find the net force once the block is already sliding.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: A 6 kg block rests on an incline of \( 37° \) with the horizontal, where \( \mu_s=0.9 \). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \), what is the actual friction force acting on the block, given that it remains at rest?
questions.explanation:
The component of the block's weight along the incline is \( mg\sin37°=6\times10\times\tfrac35=36 \) N, pulling it down the slope.

The maximum possible static friction is \( f_{s,max}=\mu_sN=0.9\times\left(6\times10\times\tfrac45\right)=0.9\times48=43.2 \) N, which is more than enough to prevent sliding.

Since the block stays at rest, the actual friction force simply balances the 36 N component of weight along the incline, acting up the incline — it does not need to reach its maximum possible value.
questions.hint: Since the block remains at rest, friction is not at its maximum — it simply balances the component of gravity pulling the block down the incline.
distractor_logic: Uses the maximum possible static friction rather than recognizing friction only needs to match the actual component of gravity along the incline to maintain equilibrium.
Uses the normal force value instead of the component of weight along the incline as the friction force.
Computes the difference between the maximum static friction and the driving force instead of recognizing friction simply equals the driving force here.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: A 2 kg block is pulled up a rough incline of \( 37° \) by a force of 20 N applied parallel to the incline surface. The coefficient of kinetic friction is \( \mu_k=0.25 \). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \), what is the block's acceleration up the incline?
options: 0 m/s\(^2\) — the block does not accelerate
questions.explanation:
The normal force is \( N=mg\cos37°=2\times10\times\tfrac45=16 \) N, so the kinetic friction, acting down the incline and opposing the upward motion, is \( f_k=\mu_kN=0.25\times16=4 \) N.

The component of weight along the incline, also acting down the incline, is \( mg\sin37°=2\times10\times\tfrac35=12 \) N.

The net force up the incline is \( 20-12-4=4 \) N, so the acceleration is \( a=\dfrac{4}{2}=2 \) m/s\(^2\), up the incline.
questions.hint: Since the block moves up the incline, both the weight's component along the incline and the kinetic friction act down the incline, opposing the applied force — include both when finding the net force.
distractor_logic: Forgets to include the component of gravity along the incline as an opposing force, only subtracting friction from the applied force.
Uses only the applied force divided by mass, ignoring both gravity's component along the incline and friction entirely.
Incorrectly assumes the applied force exactly balances the combined opposing forces, without actually adding up the individual opposing components to check.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: A 3 kg block on a horizontal table (\( \mu_k=0.2 \) between block and table) is connected by a light string over a smooth pulley at the table's edge to a 2 kg block hanging freely. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the acceleration of the system?
questions.explanation:
The hanging block's weight drives the motion: \( m_2g=2\times10=20 \) N.

Friction opposes the table block's motion: \( f_k=\mu_kN=\mu_km_1g=0.2\times3\times10=6 \) N.

The net force is \( 20-6=14 \) N, and since both blocks share the same acceleration magnitude, \( a=\dfrac{14}{2+3}=2.8 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: The net driving force is the hanging block's weight minus the friction force resisting the table block's motion; divide this net force by the total mass of both blocks.
distractor_logic: Ignores friction on the table block entirely, using only the hanging block's weight divided by the total mass.
Subtracts the friction force from the total mass instead of from the driving force, an incorrect way of accounting for friction.
Divides the hanging block's weight (20 N) by only its own mass (2 kg) instead of dividing the net force by the combined mass of both blocks (5 kg).

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: A graph is plotted of the friction force on a block versus the magnitude of a gradually increasing applied horizontal force, starting from zero. Which description correctly matches the shape of this graph?
options: Friction remains constant at \( \mu_sN \) for all values of the applied force, from zero upward
Friction rises linearly with the applied force indefinitely, with no upper limit
Friction remains zero until the applied force reaches \( \mu_sN \), after which it suddenly jumps to a much higher value
Friction rises linearly, equal to the applied force, up to a maximum value; beyond that point it drops slightly and remains roughly constant at the (lower) kinetic friction value as the block slides
questions.explanation:
While the block remains at rest, static friction self-adjusts to exactly equal the applied force, so the graph rises linearly along a line of slope 1, starting from the origin.

This continues up to the maximum static friction value, \( f_{s,max}=\mu_sN \), at which point the block begins to slide.

Once sliding, the friction force switches to the kinetic value \( f_k=\mu_kN \), which is typically slightly lower than \( f_{s,max} \) (since \( \mu_k<\mu_s \)), and stays roughly constant at that lower value as the applied force increases further.
questions.hint: Think about the two distinct regimes: friction matching the applied force while the object is still at rest, versus friction taking a fixed (generally lower) value once sliding begins.
distractor_logic: This ignores that static friction self-adjusts to match the applied force while the block is still at rest, rather than jumping immediately to its maximum value.
Static friction cannot increase without bound; it has a maximum value \( \mu_sN \), beyond which the object begins to slide and friction switches to the generally lower kinetic value.
This reverses the actual behavior; friction is present and equal to the applied force from the very start, and after the maximum it actually drops to the kinetic value, not a higher one.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: A car of mass 1000 kg goes around a flat, unbanked curve of radius 100 m. If the coefficient of static friction between the tires and the road is \( \mu_s=0.4 \), what is the maximum speed at which the car can take the curve without skidding? Take \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.explanation:
The maximum available centripetal force is the maximum static friction: \( f_{s,max}=\mu_smg \).

Setting this equal to the required centripetal force, \( \mu_smg=\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \), the mass cancels, giving \( v^2=\mu_sgr \).

Substituting: \( v^2=0.4\times10\times100=400 \), so \( v=\sqrt{400}=20 \) m/s.
questions.hint: The maximum centripetal force available is the maximum static friction; set this equal to \( mv^2/r \) and solve for \( v \).
distractor_logic: Forgets to take the square root, using \( \mu_sgr=400 \) directly as if it were the speed rather than the speed squared.
Mistakenly squares the radius rather than eventually taking the square root of the correctly formed product \( \mu_sgr \).
Divides \( \mu_sgr \) by an additional factor of 100 instead of taking the correct square root of 400.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: A curve of radius 120 m is banked at an angle of \( 37° \) with the horizontal. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\) and \( \tan37°=\tfrac34 \), what is the optimum speed for a vehicle to take this curve with no reliance on friction?
questions.explanation:
For a frictionless banked curve at the optimum speed, \( v=\sqrt{rg\tan\theta} \).

Substituting \( r=120 \) m, \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), and \( \tan37°=\tfrac34 \): \( v=\sqrt{120\times10\times\tfrac34}=\sqrt{900}=30 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Use \( v=\sqrt{rg\tan\theta} \), being careful to use the tangent of the given banking angle, not the sine or a different angle's tangent.
distractor_logic: Forgets to take the square root of \( rg\tan\theta \), reporting that product (900) directly as the speed.
Uses \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \) in place of \( \tan37°=\tfrac34 \) inside the square root, mixing up the two trigonometric ratios.
Mistakenly uses \( \tan45°=1 \) instead of the given \( \tan37°=\tfrac34 \), effectively treating the banking angle as \( 45° \) instead of the actual \( 37° \).

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: A car of mass \( m \) travels around a flat, horizontal curve of radius \( r \) at constant speed \( v \). Which of the following correctly lists all the distinct forces acting on the car?
options: Weight (down), normal force from the road (up), friction from the road (horizontal, toward the center), and a separate centripetal force (also horizontal, toward the center)
Weight (down) and a centripetal force (horizontal, toward the center) only, with no normal force or friction
Weight (down), normal force from the road (up), and friction from the road (horizontal, toward the center)
Weight (down), normal force from the road (up), and a centrifugal force pushing the car outward
questions.explanation:
The car has exactly three real forces acting on it: its weight (from gravity), the normal force from the road (perpendicular to the road surface), and friction from the road (parallel to the road surface, here directed toward the center to provide the turning effect).

Friction is itself the centripetal force in this situation — it should never be listed as a separate, additional force alongside itself.

There is also no real 'centrifugal force' acting on the car in this inertial (ground) frame; that apparent outward effect only arises as a fictitious force if analyzed from a frame of reference that is itself rotating with the car.
questions.hint: List only the genuinely real forces acting on the car from other objects (the road, gravity) — don't add a separate arrow just because the motion happens to be circular.
distractor_logic: This double-counts the centripetal force; friction is already the real force supplying the center-directed acceleration here, so adding a separate 'centripetal force' arrow counts the same physical force twice.

This omits the very real normal force, which balances the car's weight vertically, and incorrectly replaces friction with an invented 'centripetal force' rather than recognizing friction itself as the actual centripetal force here.

Centrifugal force is a fictitious force that only appears in a rotating (non-inertial) reference frame; in the ordinary ground-based inertial frame used for this problem, no such outward force actually acts on the car.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: A small ball of mass 1 kg is attached to a string of length 2 m and whirled in a horizontal circle so that the string makes a constant angle of \( 37° \) with the vertical (a conical pendulum). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \), what is the tension in the string?
questions.explanation:
For the conical pendulum, the vertical component of the tension balances the weight: \( T\cos37°=mg \).

So \( T=\dfrac{mg}{\cos37°}=\dfrac{1\times10}{4/5}=12.5 \) N.
questions.hint: The vertical component of the tension must balance the entire weight of the ball; use this to solve for the full tension.
distractor_logic: Reports the ball's weight directly as the tension, ignoring that only the vertical component of the tension balances the weight.
Uses \( mg\cos37° \) directly as the tension instead of correctly dividing the weight by \( \cos37° \).
Uses \( mg\sin37° \) in place of the correct calculation, confusing it with the horizontal (centripetal) component of the tension rather than the full tension itself.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: For the same conical pendulum (string length 2 m, angle \( 37° \) with the vertical, \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \)), what is the radius of the horizontal circular path traced by the ball?
questions.explanation: The string traces out a cone, with the ball moving in a horizontal circle whose radius is the horizontal component of the string's length: \( r=L\sin37°=2\times\tfrac35=1.2 \) m.
questions.hint: The radius of the horizontal circle is the horizontal component of the string's length, found using the sine of the angle from the vertical.
distractor_logic: Uses the full string length as the radius, ignoring that the ball traces a smaller horizontal circle since the string is tilted at an angle from the vertical.
Uses \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \) instead of \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), confusing the horizontal and vertical components of the string's length.
Squares the sine value (\( \sin^237°=0.36 \)) and multiplies by the length, instead of using \( \sin37° \) directly to find the radius.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: For the same conical pendulum (mass 1 kg, string length 2 m, angle \( 37° \) with the vertical, tension 12.5 N, radius 1.2 m, \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \)), what is the speed of the ball as it moves around the circle?
questions.explanation:
The horizontal component of the tension supplies the centripetal force: \( T\sin37°=\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \).

Substituting, \( 12.5\times\tfrac35=7.5 \) N \( =\dfrac{1\times v^2}{1.2} \), so \( v^2=7.5\times1.2=9 \).

Taking the square root, \( v=3 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Use the horizontal component of the tension as the centripetal force, \( F=mv^2/r \), and solve for \( v \).
distractor_logic: Reports the horizontal component of the tension (7.5 N) directly as if it were the speed, rather than using it to solve for \( v \) via \( F=mv^2/r \).
Reports \( v^2=9 \) directly as the speed, forgetting to take the square root.
Divides the correctly found \( v^2=9 \) by an extra factor before taking the square root, rather than taking the square root of 9 directly.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: A ball attached to a string of length 10 m is whirled in a vertical circle. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the minimum speed the ball must have at the topmost point of the circle so that the string does not go slack?
questions.explanation:
At the topmost point, both gravity and the string tension point downward, toward the center.

At the minimum speed, the tension is exactly zero, and gravity alone supplies the full centripetal force: \( mg=\dfrac{mv_{min}^2}{r} \), so \( v_{min}=\sqrt{gr} \).

Substituting \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\) and \( r=10 \) m: \( v_{min}=\sqrt{10\times10}=\sqrt{100}=10 \) m/s.
questions.hint: At the minimum speed, the string tension drops to exactly zero, and gravity alone supplies the entire centripetal force at the top.
distractor_logic: Reports \( v^2=gr=100 \) directly as the speed, forgetting to take the square root.
Uses \( v=2\sqrt{gr} \)-style doubling instead of the correct \( v=\sqrt{gr} \).
Divides \( gr \) by an incorrect extra factor of 100 before taking the square root, rather than the correct value of 100.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: A 2 kg ball attached to a string of length 1 m moves in a vertical circle. At the lowest point of the circle, its speed is 5 m/s. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the tension in the string at this lowest point?
questions.explanation:
At the lowest point, the center of the circle is directly above the ball, so the tension acts upward (toward the center) and gravity acts downward (away from the center).

Newton's second law along the radial direction gives \( T-mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \), so \( T=mg+\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \).

Substituting \( m=2 \) kg, \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( v=5 \) m/s, \( r=1 \) m: \( T=2\times10+\dfrac{2\times25}{1}=20+50=70 \) N.
questions.hint: At the bottom of a vertical circle, both the tension (upward, toward the center) and gravity (downward) act; the net upward force must supply the centripetal force.
distractor_logic: Uses only the centripetal force term (\( mv^2/r \)) as the tension, forgetting to also include the weight of the ball.
Uses only the ball's weight as the tension, forgetting to include the additional centripetal force term needed at the bottom of the loop.
Subtracts the centripetal force term from the weight instead of adding them, as though the two contributions opposed each other at the bottom of the circle.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A time-varying force \( F(t)=6t \) N (with \( t \) in seconds) acts on a 2 kg block initially at rest. What is the block's speed at \( t=3 \) s?
questions.explanation:
The impulse delivered is \( J=\displaystyle\int_0^3 6t\,dt=\left[3t^2\right]_0^3=3\times9=27 \) N s.

This impulse equals the change in momentum, so \( \Delta p=27 \) kg m/s.

Since the block starts from rest, its speed at \( t=3 \) s is \( v=\dfrac{\Delta p}{m}=\dfrac{27}{2}=13.5 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Since the force depends on time, find the impulse by integrating \( F(t) \) over the interval, then divide by mass to get the velocity.
distractor_logic: Computes the impulse as \( F(3)\times3 \), treating the force as constant at its final value, instead of integrating \( F(t) \) over time.
Integrates incorrectly as \( \int6\,dt \), dropping the \( t \) dependence, instead of \( \int6t\,dt \).
Correctly integrates to find the impulse as 27 N s but forgets to divide by the mass to obtain velocity.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: The momentum of a 1 kg particle varies with time as \( p(t)=3t^2-2t \) (in kg m/s, \( t \) in seconds). What is the magnitude of the net force acting on the particle at \( t=2 \) s?
questions.explanation:
Newton's second law gives \( F=\dfrac{dp}{dt} \).

Differentiating, \( \dfrac{dp}{dt}=6t-2 \).

At \( t=2 \) s, \( F=6(2)-2=10 \) N.
questions.hint: Force is the time derivative of momentum, \( F=dp/dt \), not momentum divided by time.
distractor_logic: Evaluates \( p(2) \) itself, giving the momentum, instead of differentiating \( p(t) \) to find the force.
Differentiates the \( 3t^2 \) term correctly to get \( 6t \) but drops the derivative of the \( -2t \) term, evaluating \( 6\times2 \) without subtracting 2.
Computes \( p(2)/t \) as if force were momentum divided by time, instead of differentiating \( p(t) \) with respect to time.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A 2 kg mass at rest is acted on by two constant forces, \( \vec{F}_1=(6,8) \) N and \( \vec{F}_2=(2,-2) \) N. What is the magnitude of the mass's velocity after 2 s?
questions.explanation:
Adding the forces componentwise, \( \vec{F}_{net}=(6+2,\ 8-2)=(8,6) \) N, which has magnitude \( |\vec{F}_{net}|=\sqrt{8^2+6^2}=\sqrt{100}=10 \) N.

The acceleration magnitude is \( a=\dfrac{F_{net}}{m}=\dfrac{10}{2}=5 \) m/s\(^2\).

Starting from rest, the speed after \( t=2 \) s is \( v=at=5\times2=10 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Add the two force vectors componentwise first, then use \( a=F_{net}/m \) and \( v=at \).
distractor_logic: Correctly computes the acceleration as 5 m/s\(^2\) but reports that number as the final velocity, forgetting to multiply by the elapsed time.
Multiplies the net force magnitude directly by the time without first dividing by mass, effectively skipping the acceleration step.
Combines only the y-components of the two forces (8 and -2) into the net force, ignoring the x-components entirely.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A ball of mass 0.5 kg falls and strikes the floor with a downward speed of 6 m/s, then rebounds straight up with a speed of 4 m/s. If the ball is in contact with the floor for 0.05 s, what is the average force exerted by the floor on the ball?
questions.explanation:
Taking upward as positive, the ball's momentum just before impact is \( p_i=-0.5\times6=-3 \) kg m/s (downward), and just after is \( p_f=+0.5\times4=+2 \) kg m/s (upward).

The change in momentum is \( \Delta p=p_f-p_i=2-(-3)=5 \) kg m/s.

The average force is \( F=\dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{5}{0.05}=100 \) N, directed upward, consistent with the floor pushing the ball back up.
questions.hint: Take a consistent positive direction (say, upward) and carefully compute the momentum before and after the bounce, including signs, before dividing by the contact time.
distractor_logic: Treats both speeds as being in the same direction and simply subtracts them (6-4=2 m/s), undercounting the actual reversal in momentum.
Uses only the incoming momentum magnitude (\( 0.5\times6=3 \) kg m/s) as if that alone were the momentum change, ignoring the outgoing momentum.
Uses only the outgoing momentum magnitude (\( 0.5\times4=2 \) kg m/s) as the momentum change, and also assigns the force the wrong direction.

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A 5 kg block starts from rest and is pushed by a constant horizontal force of 10 N for 4 s. The force is then reversed in direction (same magnitude) and applied for another 4 s. What is the block's velocity at the end of this second interval?
questions.explanation:
In the first 4 s, the acceleration is \( a_1=\dfrac{F}{m}=\dfrac{10}{5}=2 \) m/s\(^2\), so the velocity at the end of this interval is \( v_1=a_1t=2\times4=8 \) m/s.

When the force reverses, the acceleration becomes \( a_2=-2 \) m/s\(^2\). Over the next 4 s, \( v_2=v_1+a_2t=8+(-2)(4)=0 \) m/s.

The block is therefore momentarily at rest at the end of the second interval.
questions.hint: Find the velocity gained in the first interval, then apply the reversed (now negative) acceleration for the second interval starting from that velocity.
distractor_logic: Applies the same forward acceleration for the full 8 s, ignoring that the force reverses direction for the second 4 s interval.
Correctly finds the velocity after the first 4 s but wrongly assumes the velocity stays constant once the force reverses, rather than continuing to decelerate.

Incorrectly adds the magnitudes of the forward and reversed accelerations (2 m/s\(^2\)+2 m/s\(^2\)=4 m/s\(^2\)) as the deceleration for the second interval, instead of using only the reversed acceleration of 2 m/s\(^2\).

questions.topic: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
questions.question: A force \( F(t)=20\left(1-\dfrac{t}{4}\right) \) N (with \( t \) in seconds) acts on a 4 kg object starting from rest, for \( 0\le t\le4 \) s. What is the object's speed at \( t=4 \) s?
questions.explanation:
The force decreases linearly from 20 N at \( t=0 \) to 0 N at \( t=4 \) s, so its graph is a triangle of base 4 s and height 20 N.

The impulse is the area of this triangle: \( J=\tfrac12\times4\times20=40 \) N s.

Since the object starts from rest, its speed at \( t=4 \) s is \( v=\dfrac{J}{m}=\dfrac{40}{4}=10 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Recognize that the force-time graph is a triangle decreasing linearly from 20 N to 0; the impulse is the area of that triangle, and velocity follows from dividing impulse by mass.
distractor_logic: Treats the force as constant at its initial value of 20 N over the full 4 s, ignoring that it decreases linearly to zero, giving an inflated impulse of 80 N s before dividing by mass.
Correctly computes the impulse as 40 N s (the area of the triangular force-time graph) but then divides by \( 2m \) instead of \( m \).
Correctly finds the impulse as 40 N s but reports it directly as the velocity, forgetting to divide by the mass.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: A firecracker of mass 3 kg, initially at rest, explodes into two fragments. One fragment of mass 1 kg flies off with velocity \( (8,0) \) m/s. What is the velocity vector of the other (2 kg) fragment?
options: \( (-4,0) \) m/s — i.e. 4 m/s directly opposite to the first fragment
questions.explanation:
Before the explosion, the firecracker is at rest, so the total momentum of the system is zero.

Momentum conservation requires \( m_1\vec{v}_1+m_2\vec{v}_2=\vec{0} \), so \( 1\times(8,0)+2\times\vec{v}_2=(0,0) \).

Solving, \( \vec{v}_2=\left(\dfrac{-8}{2},\ \dfrac{0}{2}\right)=(-4,0) \) m/s — that is, 4 m/s directly opposite to the first fragment's motion.
questions.hint: The total momentum of the firecracker system was zero before the explosion, and momentum is conserved through the explosion — set the vector sum of the two fragments' momenta to zero.
distractor_logic: Uses the first fragment's velocity directly for the second fragment, ignoring that the second fragment has twice the mass and so must move at half the speed for momentum to balance.
Divides the first fragment's momentum by the total mass (3 kg) instead of by the second fragment's own mass (2 kg).
Invents a nonzero y-component for the second fragment even though the first fragment's momentum, and hence the required balancing momentum, has no y-component at all.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: A 0.4 kg ball moving at 10 m/s strikes a heavy wall perpendicularly and rebounds elastically with the same speed. The ball is in contact with the wall for 0.02 s. By Newton's third law, what average force does the ball exert on the wall during the impact?
options: 0 N — since the ball rebounds with the same speed, there is no net force at all
400 N, directed away from the wall
questions.explanation:
Taking the ball's initial direction (toward the wall) as positive, its momentum changes from \( +0.4\times10=4 \) kg m/s to \( -0.4\times10=-4 \) kg m/s.

The change in momentum has magnitude \( \Delta p=4-(-4)=8 \) kg m/s, so the force the wall exerts on the ball is \( F=\dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{8}{0.02}=400 \) N, directed away from the wall.

By Newton's third law, the ball exerts an equal and opposite force of 400 N on the wall, directed into the wall.
questions.hint: First find the force the wall exerts on the ball from its momentum change (accounting for the direction reversal), then apply Newton's third law for the force on the wall.
distractor_logic: This confuses the ball's unchanged speed with there being no force; the ball's velocity direction reverses, so its momentum changes substantially even though its speed does not.
Uses only the ball's incoming momentum (4 kg m/s) instead of the full momentum change that accounts for the reversal in direction (8 kg m/s).

Finds the correct magnitude but assigns the reaction force on the wall in the wrong direction; by Newton's third law, the ball must push into the wall, opposite to the force the wall exerts on the ball.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: A 2 kg block moving at 5 m/s collides with and sticks to a stationary 3 kg block over a very short collision time of 0.01 s. During this same 0.01 s, a constant external horizontal force of 400 N (from a separate applied push, unrelated to the collision) also acts on the 2 kg block. Should momentum conservation, ignoring the 400 N force, be used to find the common velocity after the collision?
options: No — the 400 N force delivers an impulse of 4 kg m/s in just 0.01 s, which is not negligible compared to the block's initial momentum of 10 kg m/s, so it must be included
Yes — any force that is not part of the collision itself is automatically negligible during a collision
No — momentum conservation can never be applied to any system that experiences friction, applied pushes, or any other outside force, however small
Yes — the 400 N force acts only on the 2 kg block internally, so it does not count as an external force on the system
questions.explanation:
The impulse delivered by the 400 N force during the 0.01 s collision is \( J=400\times0.01=4 \) kg m/s.

This is 40% of the 2 kg block's initial momentum of \( 2\times5=10 \) kg m/s — far too large to neglect, unlike the case of ordinary friction whose impulse over such a short time is typically negligible.

Because this external force is significant, momentum conservation for the two-block system cannot be applied while ignoring it; the force must be included in a full Newton's-second-law analysis of the system.
questions.hint: Compare the impulse the extra force delivers during the collision time to the momentum already present in the system — is it small enough to neglect, or not?
distractor_logic: This wrongly assumes all non-collision forces are always negligible; whether a force can be ignored depends on comparing its impulse to the momentum involved, not merely on whether it is part of the collision.
This overstates the restriction; sufficiently small external impulses, like ordinary friction during a brief collision, genuinely can be neglected as a good approximation.
This misclassifies the force; a force applied by something outside the two-block system is external to the system regardless of which single block within the system it happens to act on.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: Two blocks of mass 4 kg and 6 kg are connected by a light, inextensible string, and an external horizontal force of 30 N is applied to the 6 kg block (leading) on a frictionless floor. When finding the common acceleration using the whole two-block system, the tension \( T \) is correctly excluded as an internal force. If the 6 kg block is now analyzed on its own, should \( T \) be included in its force equation?
options: No — since \( T \) was correctly excluded for the full system, it must also be excluded for any smaller part of that same system
Yes — for the 6 kg block alone, the string crosses the boundary of that smaller system, so \( T \) is a genuine external force on it and must be included
No — tension can never appear in a single block's equation of motion, only in equations for the combined system
Yes, but only if the string has some mass; for a truly massless string, \( T \) is never a real force on either block
questions.explanation:
When both blocks are treated together as one 10 kg system, the two tension forces (one on each block, from the same string) are equal and opposite and act only between the blocks, so they are internal to that combined system and are correctly excluded from \( F_{net,ext}=Ma \) for the system as a whole.

But once the 6 kg block is isolated as its own smaller system, the string now crosses that system's boundary, so the tension \( T \) it exerts on the 6 kg block is a genuine external force on that block and must appear in its own equation: \( 30-T=6a \).

The same physical force can be internal to a larger system and external to a smaller one, depending entirely on where the system's boundary is drawn.
questions.hint: A force is 'internal' only relative to the boundary of the system you've chosen — the whole two-block system, or just one block within it.
distractor_logic: This wrongly assumes 'internal' is a fixed property of the force itself, rather than something that depends on which boundary — the whole system or a single block — is being analyzed.
The opposite is true; tension is precisely the kind of force that must appear when isolating one connected block, since it is what that block actually feels from the string.
A massless string's tension is still a completely real force felt by each block it is attached to; masslessness only ensures the tension is the same at both ends, not that the force disappears.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: A 50 kg boy standing on a stationary 200 kg cart (which can move freely on frictionless rails) throws a 2 kg ball horizontally forward at 15 m/s (relative to the ground). What is the recoil speed of the (boy + cart) system just after the throw?
options: 0.6 m/s, opposite to the direction the ball was thrown
15 m/s, opposite to the direction the ball was thrown
0.12 m/s, opposite to the direction the ball was thrown
0.12 m/s, in the same direction as the ball was thrown
questions.explanation:
Before the throw, the total momentum of (boy + cart + ball) is zero.

The ball's momentum after the throw is \( p_{ball}=2\times15=30 \) kg m/s, forward.

Since the boy stays on the cart, they recoil together with combined mass \( 50+200=250 \) kg, and their momentum must be equal and opposite: \( v=\dfrac{30}{250}=0.12 \) m/s, opposite to the direction the ball was thrown.
questions.hint: The (boy + cart) system recoils together as a single combined mass; use conservation of the total momentum of (boy + cart + ball), which started at zero.
distractor_logic: Divides the ball's momentum by only the boy's mass (50 kg), ignoring that the boy and cart recoil together as a combined 250 kg mass.
Assumes the (boy+cart) system must recoil at the same speed as the ball itself, ignoring the vastly different masses involved.
Gets the correct magnitude but assigns the recoil in the wrong direction; conservation of the system's zero initial momentum requires the (boy+cart) to move opposite to the ball.

questions.topic: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.question: A 1 kg block A moving at 6 m/s collides with and sticks to a stationary 2 kg block B, forming a combined block. This combined block then collides with and sticks to a stationary 2 kg block C. What is the final common velocity of all three blocks?
questions.explanation:
The total momentum of the three-block system is conserved throughout, since only internal collision forces act at each stage.

The initial total momentum is entirely due to block A: \( p_i=1\times6=6 \) kg m/s (blocks B and C start at rest).

Once all three blocks move together after both collisions, the total mass is \( 1+2+2=5 \) kg, so the final common velocity is \( v=\dfrac{6}{5}=1.2 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Since both collisions are perfectly inelastic and no external force acts, the final velocity of all three blocks can be found directly from the total initial momentum of the whole three-block system divided by the total mass — momentum is conserved through both collisions.
distractor_logic: Stops after the first collision (with block B), forgetting that the combined block then also collides with block C.
Naively averages the intermediate velocity (2 m/s, after colliding with B) and block C's initial velocity (0 m/s) without weighting by their different masses.
Divides the correct total momentum of 6 kg m/s by an incomplete total mass of 4 kg, having missed part of the combined mass when accounting for all three blocks.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: A 60 kg person stands on a weighing scale inside an elevator that is accelerating upward at 2 m/s\(^2\). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what does the scale read?
questions.explanation:
Taking upward as positive, Newton's second law for the person gives \( N-mg=ma \), so \( N=m(g+a) \).

Substituting \( m=60 \) kg, \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( a=2 \) m/s\(^2\): \( N=60\times(10+2)=720 \) N.

Since the elevator accelerates upward, the scale reads more than the person's actual weight of 600 N.
questions.hint: The scale reads the normal force on the person; apply Newton's second law to the person, noting the net upward force must produce the given upward acceleration.
distractor_logic: Reports the person's actual weight \( mg \), ignoring that the elevator's upward acceleration increases the scale reading above the true weight.
Incorrectly subtracts the acceleration term instead of adding it, as if the elevator were accelerating downward rather than upward.
Uses only \( ma \), the extra force due to acceleration, as the entire scale reading, forgetting to include the person's actual weight \( mg \).

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: An elevator of mass 500 kg (including any load) accelerates downward at 2 m/s\(^2\) while being lowered by a cable. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the tension in the cable?
questions.explanation:
Taking downward as positive, Newton's second law for the elevator gives \( mg-T=ma \), so \( T=m(g-a) \).

Substituting \( m=500 \) kg, \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( a=2 \) m/s\(^2\): \( T=500\times(10-2)=4000 \) N.

Since the elevator accelerates downward, the cable tension is less than the elevator's actual weight of 5000 N, but still nonzero since the acceleration is smaller than \( g \).
questions.hint: Apply Newton's second law to the elevator, taking care with the sign of the acceleration since the elevator accelerates downward but the cable still provides some support.
distractor_logic: Reports the elevator's actual weight \( mg \), ignoring that the downward acceleration reduces the required cable tension below the full weight.
Uses only \( ma \) as the entire tension, forgetting to include the elevator's actual weight in the calculation.
Adds \( ma \) to \( mg \) instead of subtracting it, as if the elevator were accelerating upward rather than downward.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: A small ball of mass 2 kg is held in equilibrium against a smooth, frictionless vertical wall by a light string attached to the wall above the ball. The string makes an angle of \( 37° \) with the vertical wall. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \), what is the normal force exerted by the wall on the ball?
questions.explanation:
Vertical equilibrium requires the string's vertical component to balance the weight: \( T\cos37°=mg \), so \( T=\dfrac{mg}{\cos37°}=\dfrac{2\times10}{4/5}=25 \) N.

Horizontal equilibrium requires the wall's normal force to balance the string's horizontal component: \( N=T\sin37°=25\times\tfrac35=15 \) N.
questions.hint: Resolve the string's tension into vertical and horizontal components; the vertical component must balance the weight, and the horizontal component equals the normal force.
distractor_logic: Reports the ball's weight directly as the normal force, ignoring that only part of the string's tension acts horizontally.
Reports the string's tension instead of the normal force, confusing the two different forces.
Uses \( mg\sin37° \) directly (with \( mg \) instead of the string's tension \( T \)) as the horizontal force, skipping the correct step of first solving for \( T \) from vertical equilibrium.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: Three blocks of masses 2 kg, 3 kg, and 5 kg are connected in a line by two light strings on a frictionless floor, in the order 2 kg — string A — 3 kg — string B — 5 kg. A horizontal force of 40 N is applied to the 5 kg block, pulling all three blocks together. What is the tension in string A, connecting the 2 kg and 3 kg blocks?
questions.explanation:
The common acceleration of the whole 10 kg system is \( a=\dfrac{F}{m_{total}}=\dfrac{40}{10}=4 \) m/s\(^2\).

String A only needs to pull the 2 kg block (the block farthest from the applied force), so applying Newton's second law to just that block: \( T_A=m_1a=2\times4=8 \) N.

(For comparison, string B must pull both the 2 kg and 3 kg blocks together, giving \( T_B=(2+3)\times4=20 \) N — a larger tension, since it carries more mass.)
questions.hint: Find the common acceleration of the whole three-block system first, then isolate just the block (or blocks) on the far side of the string in question and apply Newton's second law to only that portion.
distractor_logic: Assumes the entire applied force is transmitted all the way back through both strings to the first block, ignoring that the force needed depends only on the mass beyond each string.
Computes the tension in string B, which must accelerate the combined 2+3=5 kg mass ahead of it, instead of string A, which only needs to accelerate the 2 kg block.
Mistakenly applies the acceleration to an incorrect mass of 4 kg instead of correctly isolating just the 2 kg block that string A alone must pull.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: Two blocks of mass 1 kg and 4 kg are connected by a spring of spring constant 50 N/m on a frictionless floor (1 kg block in front). A horizontal force of 10 N is applied to the rear (4 kg) block, and the system moves with a common acceleration once the spring's extension has stabilized at a constant value. What is that steady extension of the spring?
questions.explanation:
The common acceleration of the whole 5 kg system is \( a=\dfrac{F}{m_{total}}=\dfrac{10}{5}=2 \) m/s\(^2\).

At a constant (steady) extension, the spring exerts a constant force, which for the front 1 kg block alone must equal \( F_{spring}=m_1a=1\times2=2 \) N (the only horizontal force on it).

By Hooke's law, the extension is \( x=\dfrac{F_{spring}}{k}=\dfrac{2}{50}=0.04 \) m.
questions.hint: At the steady (constant) extension, the spring force equals whatever net force is needed to accelerate just the front block at the system's common acceleration.
distractor_logic: Uses the full applied force of 10 N directly in \( x=F/k \), instead of the smaller spring force needed to accelerate only the front 1 kg block.
Uses the rear 4 kg block's required force (\( 4\times2=8 \) N) instead of the front block's required force to compute the spring's extension.

Combines the applied force and spring constant with an incorrect extra factor of the front block's mass, instead of first finding the correct spring force from the front block's mass and acceleration.

questions.topic: Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force
questions.question: A 2 kg block rests on a frictionless incline of angle \( 37° \) with the horizontal. It is connected by a light string, over a smooth pulley fixed at the top of the incline, to a 3 kg block hanging vertically off the side. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \), what is the acceleration of the system, given that the hanging block descends, pulling the other block up the incline?
questions.explanation:
The hanging block's weight, \( m_2g=3\times10=30 \) N, drives the motion.

Opposing it is the component of the incline block's weight along the incline surface, \( m_1g\sin37°=2\times10\times\tfrac35=12 \) N.

The net force is \( 30-12=18 \) N, and since both blocks share the same acceleration magnitude (connected by an inextensible string), \( a=\dfrac{18}{2+3}=3.6 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: The net driving force is the hanging block's weight minus the component of the incline block's weight along the incline surface; divide this net force by the total mass of both blocks.
distractor_logic: Uses only the hanging block's weight (30 N) divided by the total mass (5 kg), ignoring the opposing component of the incline block's weight along the incline.
Divides the net force by only the hanging block's own mass (3 kg) instead of the total mass of both blocks (5 kg).
Uses \( m_1g\cos37° \) instead of \( m_1g\sin37° \) as the incline block's opposing force, confusing the component perpendicular to the incline with the component along it.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: A 5 kg block on a horizontal floor (\( \mu_s=0.5 \)) is pulled by a force of 20 N directed at \( 37° \) above the horizontal. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \), what is the normal force on the block from the floor?
questions.explanation:
The applied force's vertical component is \( 20\sin37°=20\times\tfrac35=12 \) N, directed upward (since the force is angled above horizontal), partially lifting the block.

Vertical equilibrium requires \( N+20\sin37°=mg \), so \( N=mg-20\sin37°=50-12=38 \) N.

This is less than the block's actual weight of 50 N, since part of the applied force is helping to support the block.
questions.hint: The applied force has both a horizontal and a vertical component; the vertical component changes how hard the block presses on the floor, and so changes the normal force away from simply \( mg \).
distractor_logic: Uses the block's full weight as the normal force, ignoring that the upward vertical component of the applied force reduces how hard the block presses on the floor.
Adds the vertical component of the applied force to the weight instead of subtracting it, as if the applied force pushed the block down rather than lifted it slightly.
Uses only the horizontal component of the applied force in place of the normal force, confusing it with an unrelated quantity.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: For the same block (5 kg, \( \mu_s=0.5 \), \( \mu_k=0.4 \), pulled by 20 N at \( 37° \) above horizontal, \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), normal force 38 N), does the block start to slide?
options: Yes — the full 20 N applied force exceeds the maximum static friction of 19 N, so the block slides
No — but only because static friction can adjust to match any applied force, however large
Yes — comparing the horizontal component (16 N) to the maximum kinetic friction (\( \mu_kN=15.2 \) N) shows the applied force is larger, so the block slides
No — the horizontal component of the applied force (16 N) is less than the maximum static friction (19 N), so the block remains at rest
questions.explanation:
The horizontal component of the applied force is \( 20\cos37°=20\times\tfrac45=16 \) N.

The maximum static friction, using the correctly reduced normal force of 38 N, is \( f_{s,max}=\mu_sN=0.5\times38=19 \) N.

Since the horizontal component (16 N) is less than this maximum (19 N), the block does not slide, and the actual friction force simply equals 16 N to keep the block in equilibrium.
questions.hint: Only the horizontal component of the applied force actually needs to overcome friction to cause horizontal sliding — and remember to use the maximum static (not kinetic) friction to decide whether motion begins at all.
distractor_logic: This incorrectly compares the maximum friction to the entire applied force rather than to only its horizontal component (16 N), which is the part that must actually overcome friction for horizontal sliding to begin.
This reaches the correct conclusion for the wrong reason; static friction does have a genuine upper limit (19 N here) that simply is not exceeded in this case, rather than being limitless.

This incorrectly uses the kinetic friction coefficient to decide whether sliding begins; the correct threshold for whether motion starts at all is the maximum static friction, not the kinetic friction value.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: In an experiment, a horizontal force of 45 N is required to just start a 6 kg block sliding on a horizontal floor. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the angle of repose for the same block-floor surface pair, using \( \tan37°=\tfrac34 \)?
questions.explanation:
From the horizontal experiment, the maximum static friction equals the force needed to just start sliding: \( f_{s,max}=45 \) N, with normal force \( N=mg=6\times10=60 \) N.

So \( \mu_s=\dfrac{f_{s,max}}{N}=\dfrac{45}{60}=0.75 \).

Since the angle of repose satisfies \( \tan\theta=\mu_s \), and \( \tan37°=\tfrac34=0.75 \), the angle of repose is \( \theta=37° \).
questions.hint: First find \( \mu_s \) from the horizontal-surface experiment using \( f_{s,max}=\mu_sN \), then use \( \tan\theta=\mu_s \) to find the angle of repose.
distractor_logic: Mistakes the numeric value of the applied force (45 N) for the angle in degrees, an unrelated coincidence of numbers.
Correctly finds \( \mu_s=0.75 \) but incorrectly matches it to \( \tan53°=\tfrac43 \) instead of \( \tan37°=\tfrac34 \).
Misplaces the decimal point, reporting \( \mu_s \) as 75 instead of 0.75, and then treats that number directly as the angle in degrees.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: A 2 kg block on an incline of \( 37° \) (with \( \mu_k=0.25 \) between block and incline) is connected by a light string over a smooth pulley at the top of the incline to a 3 kg block hanging vertically. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \), what is the acceleration of the system, given that the hanging block descends, pulling the other block up the incline?
questions.explanation:
The hanging block's weight drives the motion: \( m_2g=3\times10=30 \) N.

Opposing it are the incline block's weight component along the slope, \( m_1g\sin37°=2\times10\times\tfrac35=12 \) N, and the kinetic friction, \( f_k=\mu_k(m_1g\cos37°)=0.25\times\left(2\times10\times\tfrac45\right)=0.25\times16=4 \) N.

The net force is \( 30-12-4=14 \) N, so the acceleration is \( a=\dfrac{14}{2+3}=2.8 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: The net driving force is the hanging block's weight minus both the incline block's weight component along the slope and the kinetic friction opposing its motion; divide by the total mass of both blocks.
distractor_logic: Correctly accounts for the incline block's weight component but forgets to include friction as an additional opposing force.
Ignores both the incline block's weight component along the incline and friction, using only the hanging block's weight divided by the total mass.
Mistakenly includes the full normal force (16 N) as an additional resistance, rather than only the friction force (\( \mu_kN=4 \) N) calculated from it.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: A 4 kg block sits on an incline of \( 53° \) with the horizontal, where \( \mu_s=0.5 \). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin53°=\tfrac45 \), \( \cos53°=\tfrac35 \), what is the minimum force, applied parallel to the incline and directed up the slope, needed to keep the block from sliding down?
questions.explanation:
The weight component pulling the block down the incline is \( mg\sin53°=4\times10\times\tfrac45=32 \) N, and the normal force is \( N=mg\cos53°=4\times10\times\tfrac35=24 \) N, giving a maximum static friction of \( f_{s,max}=\mu_sN=0.5\times24=12 \) N.

At the minimum applied force needed to just prevent sliding down, friction acts at its maximum value, up the incline, assisting the applied force: \( F_{min}+f_{s,max}=mg\sin53° \).

So \( F_{min}=32-12=20 \) N.
questions.hint: At the minimum force needed to prevent sliding down, friction is at its maximum and acts up the incline, assisting the applied force — so the applied force only needs to make up the remaining difference.
distractor_logic: Ignores that friction itself can also act up the incline to help support the block, assuming the entire weight component must be balanced by the applied force alone.
Adds the maximum friction to the weight component instead of subtracting it, as though friction opposed the applied force rather than assisting it at this minimum-force threshold.
Combines the normal force and friction value in an unrelated way rather than correctly relating the weight component, friction, and applied force along the incline.

questions.topic: Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose
questions.question: A 2 kg block is given an initial speed of 8 m/s up a rough incline of \( 37° \), where \( \mu_k=0.5 \). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \), how far up the incline does the block travel before momentarily coming to rest?
questions.explanation:
While sliding up, both gravity's component along the incline and kinetic friction act down the incline (opposing the motion), giving a total deceleration of \( a=g\sin37°+\mu_kg\cos37°=10\times\tfrac35+0.5\times10\times\tfrac45=6+4=10 \) m/s\(^2\).

Using \( v^2=u^2-2as \) with \( v=0 \) (momentarily at rest) and \( u=8 \) m/s: \( 0=8^2-2\times10\times s \).

Solving, \( s=\dfrac{64}{20}=3.2 \) m.
questions.hint: While moving up the incline, both the component of gravity along the slope and kinetic friction act to decelerate the block — add both contributions to find the total deceleration before using kinematics.
distractor_logic: Uses only the deceleration due to gravity's component along the incline (6 m/s\(^2\)), forgetting to add the additional deceleration from kinetic friction acting during the upward slide.
Uses only the deceleration due to friction (4 m/s\(^2\)), forgetting the deceleration contributed by the component of gravity along the incline.
Misapplies the kinematic formula relating speed and distance, resulting in a much smaller distance than is actually consistent with the given speed and deceleration.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: A curve of radius 20 m is banked at an angle where \( \tan\theta=\tfrac34 \) (i.e. \( \theta=37° \)), and the coefficient of static friction between the tires and road is \( \mu_s=0.5 \). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the maximum safe speed for a vehicle to take this curve without skidding outward?
questions.explanation:
For a banked curve with friction, the maximum safe speed is \( v_{max}=\sqrt{rg\left(\dfrac{\mu_s+\tan\theta}{1-\mu_s\tan\theta}\right)} \).

Substituting \( \mu_s=0.5 \), \( \tan\theta=\tfrac34 \): the numerator is \( 0.5+0.75=1.25 \) and the denominator is \( 1-0.5\times0.75=0.625 \), giving a ratio of \( \dfrac{1.25}{0.625}=2 \).

So \( v_{max}^2=rg\times2=20\times10\times2=400 \), and \( v_{max}=\sqrt{400}=20 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Use the full maximum-safe-speed formula for a banked curve with friction, \( v_{max}=\sqrt{rg\left(\dfrac{\mu_s+\tan\theta}{1-\mu_s\tan\theta}\right)} \), not the simpler frictionless-banking formula.
distractor_logic: Uses the frictionless banked-curve formula, completely ignoring the additional grip that friction provides at the maximum safe speed.
Forgets to take the square root of \( v^2=400 \), reporting that value directly as the speed.
Drops the \( (1-\mu_s\tan\theta) \) denominator entirely from the maximum-safe-speed formula, using an incomplete version of the correct expression.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: For a vehicle taking a frictionless banked curve of radius \( r \), banked at angle \( \theta \), at exactly the optimum speed \( v \), which equation correctly expresses the horizontal (radial) direction Newton's second law?
options: \( N\sin\theta-\dfrac{mv^2}{r}=0 \), with \( \dfrac{mv^2}{r} \) also required as an additional external applied force to keep the car on the road
questions.explanation:
For a vehicle on a frictionless banked curve, the only horizontal force is the horizontal component of the normal force, \( N\sin\theta \), and this alone must equal the required centripetal force \( mv^2/r \): \( N\sin\theta=\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \).

Since \( N\sin\theta \) already is the centripetal force in this situation, it should never be added to \( mv^2/r \) as if they were two separate forces — doing so double-counts the same physical quantity and does not correspond to any real physical requirement.

Similarly, the full normal force \( N \) (rather than just its horizontal component) is not equal to the centripetal force alone, since part of \( N \) is needed to balance the vehicle's weight vertically.
questions.hint: The horizontal component of the normal force is already the real force supplying the centripetal requirement — it should appear only once in the equation, not be added again separately.
distractor_logic: This double-counts the centripetal force by adding it separately on the left side even though \( N\sin\theta \) already is the real force supplying it; the equation is self-contradictory as written.
This uses the full normal force, not just its horizontal component, as though it were entirely the centripetal force, ignoring that part of \( N \) is used to support the vehicle's weight vertically.
This writes the horizontal balance correctly but then incorrectly insists an additional external centripetal force must also be supplied, again double-counting the same physical requirement.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: A car crosses the top of a convex, circular hill of radius 40 m. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), at what speed would the car just begin to lose contact with the road at the very top of the hill (i.e., the normal force there becomes zero)?
questions.explanation:
At the top of the hill, both gravity and the (still-present, if any) normal force point toward the center of the circular hill (downward, since the center is below the road at the hilltop).

Newton's second law along the radial direction gives \( mg-N=\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \).

The car loses contact exactly when \( N=0 \), so \( mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \), giving \( v=\sqrt{gr}=\sqrt{10\times40}=\sqrt{400}=20 \) m/s.
questions.hint: At the point of losing contact, the normal force becomes exactly zero, and gravity alone supplies the entire centripetal force at the top of the hill.
distractor_logic: Reports \( v^2=gr=400 \) directly as the speed, forgetting to take the square root.
Divides \( gr \) by an extra factor of 100 before taking the square root, rather than using the correct value of 400.

Mistakenly doubles the term inside the square root, as if both gravity and an additional force needed to be accounted for at the critical point, rather than recognizing that \( N=0 \) exactly at this speed.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: A curve of radius 50 m is banked at an angle where \( \tan\theta=\tfrac34 \) (\( \theta=37° \)). A car takes this curve at 25 m/s, faster than the optimum (frictionless) speed for this radius and angle. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), in which direction must friction act to prevent the car from skidding, and why?
options: Friction must act up the slope of the banking (toward the outside, higher edge), since at a speed greater than the optimum, the car tends to skid inward and downward along the bank
No friction is needed at any speed, since the banking alone always provides exactly the right centripetal force regardless of speed
Friction must act vertically downward, adding to the car's weight, to increase the normal force
Friction must act down the slope of the banking (toward the inside, lower edge), since at a speed greater than the optimum, the car tends to skid outward and up the bank, requiring extra inward force
questions.explanation:
The optimum (frictionless) speed for this curve is \( v_{opt}=\sqrt{rg\tan\theta}=\sqrt{50\times10\times0.75}=\sqrt{375}\approx19.4 \) m/s.

Since the car's actual speed of 25 m/s is greater than this optimum speed, more centripetal force is required than the banking's normal force alone can provide, so the car tends to skid outward and up the slope of the bank.

Friction must therefore act down the slope (toward the inside, lower edge of the bank) to supply this extra inward force and prevent the car from skidding outward.
questions.hint: Compare the actual speed to the optimum (frictionless) speed for this radius and angle — is more or less centripetal force needed than the banking alone provides?
distractor_logic: This reverses the actual tendency; at speeds above the optimum, the required centripetal force is greater than what the banking alone provides, so the car tends to slide outward and up the slope, not inward and down.
The banking alone provides exactly the right centripetal force only at the one specific optimum speed; at any other speed, friction (or some other force) is needed to make up the difference.
Friction acts parallel to the inclined road surface, within the banked plane, not vertically; it cannot act straight down like an additional weight.

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: A small ball of mass 0.5 kg on a frictionless horizontal table is attached to a string that passes through a hole in the center of the table and connects to a 2 kg mass hanging below, which remains stationary. The ball moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.4 m. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the speed of the ball?
questions.explanation:
Since the 2 kg hanging mass is stationary, the tension in the string equals its weight: \( T=Mg=2\times10=20 \) N.

This tension is the only horizontal force on the ball, and it supplies the centripetal force: \( T=\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \), so \( v^2=\dfrac{Tr}{m}=\dfrac{20\times0.4}{0.5}=16 \).

Taking the square root, \( v=4 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Since the hanging mass is stationary, the string's tension equals its weight; this same tension is what supplies the centripetal force for the ball on the table.
distractor_logic: Uses \( v^2=Tr/m \) but forgets to divide by the ball's mass, using an incorrect combination that doubles the correct value.
Reports \( v^2=16 \) directly as the speed, forgetting to take the square root.
Uses the hanging mass's own weight-to-mass ratio in an unrelated way instead of correctly relating the tension to the ball's centripetal motion via \( T=mv^2/r \).

questions.topic: Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads
questions.question: A curve of radius 30 m is banked at \( 45° \) (\( \tan45°=1 \)), and the coefficient of static friction between the tires and road is \( \mu_s=0.5 \). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the minimum speed at which a car can take this curve without sliding down the slope toward the inside of the curve?
options: 0 m/s — the car can be stationary without sliding at any banking angle
questions.explanation:
Below the minimum safe speed, the car tends to slide down and toward the inside of the banked curve, so friction acts up the slope to help prevent this.

The minimum speed is given by \( v_{min}=\sqrt{rg\left(\dfrac{\tan\theta-\mu_s}{1+\mu_s\tan\theta}\right)} \).

Substituting \( \tan45°=1 \), \( \mu_s=0.5 \): the numerator is \( 1-0.5=0.5 \) and the denominator is \( 1+0.5\times1=1.5 \), giving a ratio of \( \tfrac13 \).

So \( v_{min}^2=30\times10\times\tfrac13=100 \), and \( v_{min}=\sqrt{100}=10 \) m/s. (Since \( \tan45°=1>\mu_s=0.5 \), this nonzero minimum genuinely applies — for a shallower bank where \( \mu_s\ge\tan\theta \), friction alone could hold a stationary car and the minimum speed would be zero.)
questions.hint: Below the minimum speed, the car tends to slide down and inward along the bank, so friction acts up the slope; use \( v_{min}=\sqrt{rg\left(\dfrac{\tan\theta-\mu_s}{1+\mu_s\tan\theta}\right)} \), valid whenever \( \tan\theta>\mu_s \).
distractor_logic: Uses the frictionless optimum-speed formula instead of the minimum-speed formula that accounts for friction acting up the slope to help prevent sliding down.

This is only true when the friction available is at least as large as \( \tan\theta \); here \( \mu_s=0.5<\tan45°=1 \), so friction alone cannot hold a stationary car on this steep a bank, and a genuine nonzero minimum speed is required.
Forgets to take the square root of \( v_{min}^2=100 \), reporting that value directly as the speed.

questions.question: A 0.5 kg ball moving at 10 m/s strikes a wall head-on and rebounds straight back. While in contact, the ball exerts an average force of 300 N on the wall for 0.02 s. Using Newton's third law to find the force the wall exerts on the ball, what is the ball's rebound speed?
questions.explanation:
By Newton's third law, the wall exerts a force of 300 N on the ball, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the 300 N the ball exerts on the wall — directed back the way the ball came.
