The impulse delivered to the ball is \( J=300\times0.02=6 \) kg m/s, opposite to the ball's original motion.

Taking the ball's initial direction as positive, its momentum changes from \( 0.5\times10=5 \) kg m/s to \( 5-6=-1 \) kg m/s, so its rebound speed is \( \dfrac{1}{0.5}=2 \) m/s.
questions.hint: First use Newton's third law to identify the force the wall exerts on the ball, then apply the impulse-momentum theorem.

questions.question: Two blocks of mass 2 kg and 6 kg are connected by a light string over a smooth, massless pulley (an Atwood machine). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), how long does it take for the heavier block's speed to increase from 0 to 6 m/s, starting from rest?
questions.explanation:
The acceleration of the Atwood machine is \( a=\dfrac{(m_2-m_1)g}{m_1+m_2}=\dfrac{(6-2)\times10}{2+6}=\dfrac{40}{8}=5 \) m/s\(^2\).

Since the system starts from rest, \( v=at \), so \( t=\dfrac{v}{a}=\dfrac{6}{5}=1.2 \) s.
questions.hint: First find the Atwood machine's constant acceleration, then use \( v=at \), starting from rest, to find the time.

questions.question: A 4 kg block slides on a rough horizontal floor with an initial speed of 12 m/s. The coefficient of kinetic friction is \( \mu_k=0.5 \). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), how long does it take for friction to bring the block to rest?
questions.explanation:
The kinetic friction force is \( f_k=\mu_kmg=0.5\times4\times10=20 \) N, acting to decelerate the block.

By the impulse-momentum theorem, this force must remove the block's entire initial momentum: \( f_k\times t=mv \), so \( t=\dfrac{mv}{f_k}=\dfrac{4\times12}{20}=2.4 \) s.

questions.question: A 2 kg ball moves in a circle of radius 5 m. A constant tangential force of 4 N (along the direction of motion) acts on it in addition to whatever provides the centripetal force, starting from rest. How long does it take for the ball's speed to reach 6 m/s?
questions.explanation:
The tangential force produces a tangential acceleration \( a_t=\dfrac{F}{m}=\dfrac{4}{2}=2 \) m/s\(^2\), which changes the ball's speed exactly as in one-dimensional motion — the radius plays no role in this particular relationship.

Starting from rest, \( v=a_tt \), so \( t=\dfrac{6}{2}=3 \) s.
questions.hint: The tangential force changes the ball's speed exactly like an ordinary straight-line force would — the radius is not needed to relate a tangential force to a change in speed.

questions.question: Two blocks of mass 3 kg and 2 kg are connected by a light string on a frictionless floor (3 kg block in front), pulled by a horizontal force of 25 N applied to the rear (2 kg) block. What is the magnitude of the force the string exerts on the front block, and what is the magnitude of the reaction force (by Newton's third law) that the front block exerts back on the string?

Applying Newton's second law to just the front (3 kg) block, the only horizontal force on it is the string's tension: \( T=3\times5=15 \) N.

By Newton's third law, the front block exerts an equal and opposite force of 15 N back on the string, regardless of the block's mass.

questions.question: A 3 kg block rests on an incline of \( 37° \) with the horizontal (\( \mu_s=0.6 \)), connected by a light string over a smooth pulley at the top of the incline to a 1 kg block hanging vertically. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \), the system remains at rest. What is the magnitude and direction of the friction force on the 3 kg block?
questions.explanation:
Since the hanging 1 kg block is in equilibrium, the tension equals its weight: \( T=1\times10=10 \) N.

The 3 kg block's weight component along the incline is \( mg\sin37°=3\times10\times\tfrac35=18 \) N, pulling it down the slope, while the tension pulls it up the slope.

For equilibrium along the slope, friction must supply the remaining balance: \( f+T=mg\sin37° \), so \( f=18-10=8 \) N, directed up the incline.
questions.hint: Since the hanging block is also in equilibrium, first find the tension from its own weight, then use the incline block's equilibrium along the slope to solve for the friction force.

questions.question: A small ball of mass 0.5 kg is attached to a horizontal spring of spring constant 40 N/m, anchored at a fixed point on a frictionless horizontal table. The ball moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m, with the spring stretched by 0.1 m from its natural length to provide the necessary force. What is the ball's speed?
questions.explanation:
The spring force is \( F=kx=40\times0.1=4 \) N, and this force supplies the centripetal force: \( F=\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \).

Solving, \( v^2=\dfrac{Fr}{m}=\dfrac{4\times0.5}{0.5}=4 \).

Taking the square root, \( v=2 \) m/s.
questions.hint: The spring force, found from Hooke's law using the given extension, supplies the centripetal force; set \( kx=mv^2/r \) and solve for \( v \).

questions.question: A car of mass 800 kg takes a banked curve of radius 40 m, banked at \( 37° \) (\( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \)), at a speed of 20 m/s — greater than the curve's optimum (frictionless) speed. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what magnitude of friction force, acting down the slope toward the inside of the curve, is needed to keep the car on the curve at this speed?
questions.explanation:
With friction \( f \) acting down the slope, the equations are \( N\cos37°-f\sin37°=mg \) and \( N\sin37°+f\cos37°=\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \).

Substituting \( mg=800\times10=8000 \) N and \( \dfrac{mv^2}{r}=\dfrac{800\times20^2}{40}=8000 \) N: \( 0.8N-0.6f=8000 \) and \( 0.6N+0.8f=8000 \).

Solving this pair of simultaneous equations gives \( N=11200 \) N and \( f=1600 \) N.
questions.hint: Write both the vertical equilibrium equation and the horizontal (centripetal) equation, with the normal force and friction force as two unknowns, then solve the pair of simultaneous equations.
distractor_logic: Reports the required centripetal force (\( mv^2/r \)) directly as the friction force, without recognizing that the normal force's horizontal component also contributes to supplying the centripetal requirement.
Reports only the horizontal component of the normal force in this scenario, mistaking it for the friction force rather than solving the full pair of simultaneous equations.
Sets up the two equilibrium equations but makes a sign error when combining them, rather than correctly eliminating the normal force between the vertical and horizontal equations.

questions.question: A 10 kg gun, including its cart, is held stationary by a horizontal string attached to a wall. It fires a 0.05 kg bullet forward at 200 m/s, with the firing lasting 0.01 s. What is the average tension in the string during the firing, needed to keep the gun and cart from moving?
questions.explanation:
The bullet gains forward momentum \( p_{bullet}=0.05\times200=10 \) kg m/s.

By momentum conservation, the gun would recoil with an equal and opposite momentum if free to move — but since the string holds it in place, the string itself must supply an equal and opposite impulse to cancel this tendency, so \( J_{string}=10 \) kg m/s.

The average tension is \( T=\dfrac{J_{string}}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{10}{0.01}=1000 \) N.
questions.hint: Since the gun does not move at all, the string must supply exactly the impulse that would otherwise have gone into the gun's recoil — and by momentum conservation, that impulse equals the bullet's own momentum change.

Combines the bullet's mass directly with its momentum value in an inconsistent way, rather than correctly computing the bullet's momentum first and then dividing by the firing time.

questions.question: A 1 kg dart moving at 12 m/s embeds in a stationary 3 kg block resting on a rough floor (\( \mu_k=0.3 \)). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), how long does it take for the combined block+dart to come to rest after the dart embeds (ignore the brief embedding time itself)?

By momentum conservation, the combined speed right after embedding is \( v=\dfrac{1\times12}{1+3}=\dfrac{12}{4}=3 \) m/s.

The friction force on the combined 4 kg mass is \( f_k=\mu_k(m_{total})g=0.3\times4\times10=12 \) N, giving a deceleration of \( a=\dfrac{12}{4}=3 \) m/s\(^2\).

The time to stop is \( t=\dfrac{v}{a}=\dfrac{3}{3}=1 \) s.
questions.hint: First use momentum conservation to find the combined speed right after the dart embeds, then use the friction force on the combined mass to find the deceleration and the stopping time.

questions.question: A 2 kg block on a rough horizontal table (\( \mu_k=0.25 \)) is connected by a light string over a smooth pulley at the table's edge to a 3 kg block hanging freely. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), starting from rest, how long does it take for the system's speed to reach 5 m/s?

questions.question: A 2 kg ball on a 1 m string moves in a vertical circle. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the tension in the string at this instant?

questions.question: A vehicle of mass 50 kg takes a curve of radius 20 m, banked at an angle where \( \tan\theta=\tfrac34 \) (\( \theta=37° \), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \)), at exactly the maximum safe speed, where friction is at its limiting value with \( \mu_s=0.5 \). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the normal force on the vehicle at this maximum speed?
questions.explanation:
At the maximum safe speed, friction is at its limiting value, \( f=\mu_sN \), acting down the slope.

The equations are \( N\cos37°-f\sin37°=mg \) and \( N\sin37°+f\cos37°=\dfrac{mv_{max}^2}{r} \).

Substituting \( f=0.5N \) and \( mg=50\times10=500 \) N into the vertical equation: \( 0.8N-0.3N=500 \), giving \( N=1000 \) N (consistent with the horizontal equation as well).
questions.hint: Set up the vertical and horizontal equilibrium equations with both \( N \) and \( f \) as unknowns, substitute \( f=\mu_sN \), and solve the resulting equations for \( N \).
distractor_logic: Reports the vehicle's weight as the normal force, without accounting for how the banking angle and the additional friction force, at its maximum, together determine the actual normal force needed.
Doubles the correctly computed normal force, likely from mishandling the simultaneous equations relating \( N \) and \( f=\mu_sN \).

Adds the vehicle's weight and the required centripetal force directly together as though they combined simply, rather than correctly solving the coupled equilibrium equations with \( f=\mu_sN \) substituted in.

questions.question: A 1 kg block sits on a rotating horizontal disk at a distance of 0.3 m from the center. At a certain instant, the block moves at 3 m/s and also has a tangential acceleration of 6 m/s\(^2\), as the disk is speeding up. Friction between the block and disk (\( \mu_s=1 \)) must simultaneously supply both the centripetal force and the tangential force needed. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), is the block able to maintain contact without slipping at this instant?
options: Yes — as long as the tangential force alone (6 N) is less than the maximum friction (10 N), the block will not slip, regardless of any additional centripetal requirement
No — the centripetal force needed (30 N) alone already exceeds the maximum available friction (10 N), so the combined requirement certainly cannot be met
Yes — friction only needs to supply the centripetal force at each instant; the tangential force is instead supplied directly by the disk's rotation itself, not by friction
No — but only because the tangential force (6 N) alone exceeds the maximum friction (10 N)
questions.explanation:
The centripetal force needed is \( \dfrac{mv^2}{r}=\dfrac{1\times9}{0.3}=30 \) N, and the tangential force needed is \( ma_t=1\times6=6 \) N.

Since friction must supply both requirements simultaneously, the combined (resultant) friction needed is \( \sqrt{30^2+6^2}\approx30.6 \) N.

The maximum available friction is \( f_{s,max}=\mu_smg=1\times1\times10=10 \) N, far less than even the centripetal requirement alone, so the block cannot maintain contact without slipping.
questions.hint: Friction is the only force available, and it must supply the centripetal and tangential requirements simultaneously as their combined resultant — compare this combined requirement to the maximum available friction.
distractor_logic: This ignores that friction must supply the centripetal force and the tangential force simultaneously, as a single combined force, not as two separately checked requirements.
Friction is the only real horizontal contact force between the block and disk, so it alone must be responsible for both the centripetal and tangential requirements.

Reaches the right conclusion for an incorrect reason; 6 N does not exceed the 10 N maximum by itself — it is the centripetal requirement, and the combined resultant, that actually exceed the friction limit.

questions.question: A 5 kg object moving at 4 m/s (no friction) suddenly splits into two fragments due to an internal explosion lasting 0.02 s. One 2 kg fragment continues forward at 10 m/s. What is the magnitude of the average force that acted on the other (3 kg) fragment during the explosion?
questions.explanation:
Before the explosion, the 3 kg fragment (as part of the whole 5 kg object) has momentum \( 3\times4=12 \) kg m/s.

By momentum conservation, since the 2 kg fragment ends up with momentum \( 2\times10=20 \) kg m/s, matching the total initial momentum of \( 5\times4=20 \) kg m/s, the 3 kg fragment must end up with momentum \( 20-20=0 \) kg m/s.

The change in the 3 kg fragment's own momentum is \( 0-12=-12 \) kg m/s, so the average force on it is \( F=\dfrac{12}{0.02}=600 \) N.
questions.hint: Before the explosion, each fragment carries its own share of the total momentum, proportional to its own mass and the common velocity; find the 3 kg fragment's momentum both before and after, then use the impulse-momentum theorem.
distractor_logic: Uses the other fragment's final momentum (20 kg m/s) as this fragment's own momentum change, instead of correctly finding this fragment's own momentum change from 12 to 0 kg m/s.
Uses only the fragment's final momentum (0) in an unrelated combination with time, rather than correctly finding the change in its own momentum from before to after the explosion.

Uses the full 5 kg object's total initial momentum (20 kg m/s) as this fragment's own momentum change, rather than correctly using only its 3 kg share (12 kg m/s) of the momentum before the explosion.

questions.question: Two blocks of mass 2 kg and 3 kg are connected by a spring of spring constant 100 N/m on a frictionless floor (2 kg block in front). A horizontal force of 15 N is applied to the rear (3 kg) block, and the spring reaches a steady, constant extension. What impulse does the spring deliver to the front block over a 4 s interval, once the extension has stabilized?
questions.explanation:
The common acceleration of the whole 5 kg system is \( a=\dfrac{15}{5}=3 \) m/s\(^2\).

At the steady extension, the spring force on the front 2 kg block alone is \( F=2\times3=6 \) N.

The impulse delivered over 4 s is \( J=F\times t=6\times4=24 \) N s.
questions.hint: First find the constant spring force needed to accelerate just the front block at the system's common acceleration, then multiply this force by the given time interval.
distractor_logic: Uses the full applied force (15 N) instead of the correctly reduced spring force (6 N) acting on just the front block.
Uses the rear block's required force (\( 3\times3=9 \) N) instead of the front block's required force to compute the impulse.
Divides the correctly found spring force (6 N) by the time interval instead of multiplying force by time to find the impulse.

questions.question: A 4 kg block, initially at rest on a rough horizontal floor (\( \mu_k=0.4 \)), receives an impulse of 24 kg m/s from a sudden brief push. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), how far does the block travel before friction brings it to rest?
questions.explanation:
The initial velocity is \( v_0=\dfrac{J}{m}=\dfrac{24}{4}=6 \) m/s.

The friction deceleration is \( a=\mu_kg=0.4\times10=4 \) m/s\(^2\).

Using \( v^2=v_0^2-2as \) with \( v=0 \): \( 0=6^2-2\times4\times s \), so \( s=\dfrac{36}{8}=4.5 \) m.
questions.hint: First convert the impulse to an initial velocity using \( v=J/m \), then use kinematics with the friction-caused deceleration to find the stopping distance.
distractor_logic: Uses only half the correctly computed deceleration (2 m/s\(^2\) instead of 4 m/s\(^2\)), perhaps from forgetting to include \( g \) properly in \( \mu_kg \).
Uses the impulse value directly as the initial speed (24 m/s) without first dividing by the block's mass to find the correct initial velocity of 6 m/s.
Uses the given impulse value directly in the kinematic distance formula in place of the initial velocity, without properly converting it to a velocity first.

questions.question: A 0.5 kg ball moves in a horizontal circle of radius 2 m at a constant speed of 4 m/s. What is the magnitude of the impulse delivered to the ball as it travels through exactly half a revolution, from one point on the circle to the diametrically opposite point?
questions.explanation:
Even though the ball's speed stays constant at 4 m/s, after exactly half a revolution its velocity vector has completely reversed direction.

Taking the initial velocity as \( +v \), the final velocity is \( -v \), so the change in momentum has magnitude \( \Delta p=m|v_f-v_i|=0.5\times|(-4)-4|=0.5\times8=4 \) kg m/s.

This equals the magnitude of the impulse delivered by the centripetal force over that half-revolution.
questions.hint: Even though the speed is constant, the direction of the velocity after half a revolution is exactly reversed — find the vector difference between the initial and final momentum, not just compare their magnitudes.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly assumes that because the speed is constant, the momentum, a vector, must also be unchanged, ignoring that the velocity's direction has completely reversed after half a revolution.
Uses only the ball's own single momentum value (\( mv \)) rather than the full change in momentum, which requires accounting for the reversal in direction.
Doubles the correctly computed impulse, perhaps by mistakenly using the full circumference or a similar unrelated quantity instead of comparing only the initial and final velocity vectors.
mixed_topics: Newton's First and Second Laws: Inertia, Momentum, and Force
Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads

questions.question: A 10 kg object hangs in equilibrium from two strings attached to the ceiling, with tensions \( T_1 \) and \( T_2 \) at different angles, and weight \( mg \) acting on the object. Which pair of forces here, if any, forms a genuine Newton's third-law action-reaction pair?
options: \( T_1 \) and \( T_2 \) form a third-law pair, since together they support the object's weight
\( T_1 \) and \( mg \) form a third-law pair, since together with \( T_2 \) they add to zero

None of the three forces (\( T_1 \), \( T_2 \), and \( mg \)) form a third-law pair with each other — all three act on the same single object and are needed together for that object's own equilibrium, a completely different relationship from a third-law pair
\( T_2 \) and \( mg \) form a third-law pair, since \( mg \) is what causes the tension in the strings in the first place
questions.explanation:
All three forces act on the same single object, the hanging mass, and together happen to sum to zero because that object is in equilibrium.

This equilibrium condition is a completely different relationship from a Newton's third-law pair, which requires exactly two different bodies interacting, with equal-magnitude, oppositely-directed forces of the same type.

The true third-law partners here are elsewhere: the reaction to \( T_1 \) is the force the object exerts back on string 1, the reaction to \( T_2 \) is the force on string 2, and the reaction to \( mg \) is the object's own gravitational pull on the Earth.
questions.hint: A genuine third-law pair always involves exactly two different bodies — check whether any two of these three forces act on two different objects, or all three act on the same one.
distractor_logic: Both act on the same single body and generally have different magnitudes; a third-law pair must involve two different bodies and always has exactly equal magnitudes.
Forces adding to zero in equilibrium is a completely different relationship from a third-law pair, which requires two different bodies and does not need any other forces to be present.
Causing a force to exist is not the same as forming a third-law reaction pair with it; a genuine pair requires two different bodies and forces of the same fundamental type and equal magnitude.

Equilibrium of a Particle and Connected Bodies: Normal Force, Tension, and Spring Force

questions.question: Two blocks of mass 2 kg and 3 kg are in contact on a rough horizontal floor (\( \mu_k=0.25 \) for both), with the 3 kg block in front. A horizontal force of 20 N is applied to the rear (2 kg) block, pushing both blocks together. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the magnitude of the contact force between the two blocks, and what force does the front block exert back on the rear block, by Newton's third law?
options: Both are 7.5 N, the net force on the whole system
The rear block pushes the front block with 12 N, but the front block pushes back with only 4.5 N, its own net force
Both are 20 N, the full applied force
Both are 12 N — the rear block pushes the front block with 12 N, and by Newton's third law, the front block pushes back on the rear block with an equal 12 N
questions.explanation:
The total friction on the whole system is \( \mu_k(m_1+m_2)g=0.25\times5\times10=12.5 \) N, so the net force is \( 20-12.5=7.5 \) N, giving \( a=\dfrac{7.5}{5}=1.5 \) m/s\(^2\).

For the front (3 kg) block alone, the contact force \( N \) pushes it forward while its own friction (\( 0.25\times3\times10=7.5 \) N) opposes it: \( N-7.5=3\times1.5=4.5 \), so \( N=12 \) N.

By Newton's third law, the front block pushes back on the rear block with an equal and opposite force of 12 N.
questions.hint: First find the system's acceleration using the total net force after friction, then isolate just the front block, including its own individual friction, to solve for the contact force.
distractor_logic: Uses the net force on the entire two-block system after friction, rather than correctly isolating just the front block, including its own individual friction, to find the actual contact force.

Confuses the front block's own net force with the reaction force it exerts on the rear block; by Newton's third law, the reaction force must exactly equal the original contact force, not the front block's separate net force.
Uses the total applied force on the whole system rather than correctly accounting for friction on each block individually and isolating just the front block's own equation of motion.

questions.question: A 3 kg ball attached to a string of length 0.5 m moves in a vertical circle. At the lowest point, its speed is 4 m/s. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the magnitude of the force the ball exerts on the string at this lowest point, by Newton's third law?
questions.explanation:
At the lowest point, \( T-mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \), so \( T=mg+\dfrac{mv^2}{r}=3\times10+\dfrac{3\times16}{0.5}=30+96=126 \) N.

This is the force the string exerts on the ball.

By Newton's third law, the ball exerts an equal and opposite force of 126 N back on the string, directed downward and outward, away from the center.
questions.hint: First find the tension the string exerts on the ball at the bottom of the loop, then recall that a genuine third-law reaction pair is always exactly equal in magnitude to the original force.
distractor_logic: Uses only the centripetal force term as the force on the string, forgetting to include the ball's weight, which also contributes to the string's tension at the bottom of the loop.
Uses only the ball's weight as the force on the string, forgetting to include the additional centripetal force term needed at the bottom of the loop.
Subtracts the centripetal force term from the weight instead of adding them, as though the two contributions opposed each other at the bottom of the circle.

questions.question: A 4 kg block rests on an incline of \( 37° \) with the horizontal (\( \mu_s=0.5 \)), connected by a light string over a smooth pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass \( M \). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \), what is the maximum value of \( M \) for which the system can remain at rest?
questions.explanation:
At the maximum hanging mass \( M \), the incline block is on the verge of sliding up, so friction acts at its maximum value (\( f_{s,max}=\mu_s\times mg\cos37°=0.5\times32=16 \) N), directed down the incline.

Equilibrium along the incline requires \( Mg=mg\sin37°+f_{s,max}=24+16=40 \) N.

So \( M=\dfrac{40}{10}=4 \) kg.
questions.hint: At the maximum hanging mass, the incline block is on the verge of being pulled up the slope, so friction acts at its maximum value, down the slope, helping to resist this.
distractor_logic: Uses only the weight component along the incline (24 N) divided by \( g \), forgetting to add the additional maximum friction force that also helps resist the hanging block at the verge of sliding.
Uses only the maximum friction force (16 N) divided by \( g \), forgetting to include the incline block's own weight component along the slope.
Adds the normal force (32 N) instead of the maximum friction force (16 N) to the weight component along the incline, before dividing by \( g \).

questions.question: A small ball of mass 0.5 kg is attached to a horizontal spring of spring constant 20 N/m, anchored at a fixed point on a frictionless horizontal table. The ball moves in a circle of radius 0.8 m at a constant speed of 4 m/s. What is the extension of the spring, assuming the spring's force alone provides the centripetal force?
questions.explanation:
The centripetal force needed is \( F=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}=\dfrac{0.5\times16}{0.8}=10 \) N.

By Hooke's law, this force determines the spring's extension: \( x=\dfrac{F}{k}=\dfrac{10}{20}=0.5 \) m.
questions.hint: First find the centripetal force needed for the given speed and radius, then use Hooke's law to find the corresponding spring extension.
distractor_logic: Uses \( mv^2 \) alone, without dividing by the radius, to find the spring force, understating the required force and hence the extension.
Forgets to divide by the spring constant, using the centripetal force value directly as the extension.
Divides the centripetal force by an incorrect factor, such as the ball's mass alone, instead of by the spring constant.

questions.question: A 900 kg car takes a flat, unbanked curve of radius 60 m at a speed of 18 m/s. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the minimum coefficient of static friction between the tires and the road required for the car to make the turn without skidding?
questions.explanation:
The required centripetal force is \( \dfrac{mv^2}{r}=\dfrac{900\times18^2}{60}=\dfrac{900\times324}{60}=4860 \) N.

Setting this equal to the maximum available friction, \( \mu_smg=4860 \), so \( \mu_s=\dfrac{4860}{900\times10}=\dfrac{4860}{9000}=0.54 \).
questions.hint: Set the required centripetal force (\( mv^2/r \)) equal to the maximum available friction (\( \mu_smg \)), then solve for \( \mu_s \).
distractor_logic: Forgets to divide by the car's weight (\( mg=9000 \) N), reporting the centripetal-force-per-unit-mass value directly as the coefficient of friction.
Divides the car's weight by the required centripetal force, an inverted ratio, instead of dividing the required centripetal force by the weight.
Forgets to divide by the radius when computing the required centripetal force, using \( mv^2 \) directly before dividing by the weight.

Circular Motion Dynamics: Centripetal Force and Banking of Roads

questions.question: A 40 kg boy stands on a 60 kg stationary cart with frictionless wheels, which is held in place by a horizontal string tied to a wall in front of him. He throws a 2 kg ball horizontally at 10 m/s (relative to the ground), in the direction of the wall, and the throw takes 0.1 s. Assuming the string prevents any motion of the boy and cart, what is the average tension in the string during the throw?
questions.explanation:
The ball's momentum after the throw is \( p_{ball}=2\times10=20 \) kg m/s.

By momentum conservation, the boy+cart system would recoil with an equal and opposite momentum if unconstrained, so the string must supply an impulse of 20 kg m/s to cancel this tendency and keep them stationary.

The average tension is \( T=\dfrac{20}{0.1}=200 \) N.
questions.hint: By momentum conservation, if the string weren't there, the boy and cart would recoil with a momentum exactly equal and opposite to the ball's — the string must instead supply this same impulse to keep them stationary.
distractor_logic: Doubles the ball's momentum, effectively double-counting the ball's momentum change and the boy+cart's momentum change as separate additional impulses rather than recognizing they are equal and opposite by momentum conservation.
Uses the ball's momentum value directly as the tension, forgetting to divide by the actual duration of the throw.
Divides the ball's momentum by an incorrect time of 0.2 s rather than the actual 0.1 s duration given.

questions.question: A 2 kg block moving at 8 m/s collides with and sticks to a stationary 6 kg block on a rough floor (\( \mu_k=0.2 \)). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), how far does the combined block travel before friction brings it to rest?
questions.explanation:
By momentum conservation, the combined speed right after the collision is \( v=\dfrac{2\times8}{2+6}=\dfrac{16}{8}=2 \) m/s.

The friction deceleration is \( a=\mu_kg=0.2\times10=2 \) m/s\(^2\).

Using \( v^2=u^2-2as \) with \( v=0 \): \( 0=2^2-2\times2\times s \), so \( s=\dfrac{4}{4}=1 \) m.
questions.hint: First use momentum conservation to find the combined speed right after the collision, then use the friction-caused deceleration in a kinematic equation to find the stopping distance.
distractor_logic: Uses the pre-collision speed of the 2 kg block (8 m/s) instead of the correctly reduced combined speed after the perfectly inelastic collision.

questions.question: A 2 kg block moves in a horizontal circle of radius 1 m on a frictionless table, attached to a string, at a constant speed of 4 m/s. A 2 kg dart, moving tangentially in the same direction as the block at that instant with a speed of 10 m/s, embeds into the block. Immediately after, what is the tension in the string, assuming the combined block+dart momentarily continues in the same circle of radius 1 m at its new speed?
questions.explanation:
By momentum conservation, the combined speed right after the dart embeds is \( v=\dfrac{2\times4+2\times10}{2+2}=\dfrac{8+20}{4}=7 \) m/s.

The new tension needed to keep the combined 4 kg mass moving in the same 1 m radius circle is \( T=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}=\dfrac{4\times49}{1}=196 \) N.
questions.hint: First use momentum conservation, treating this as a collision along the instantaneous direction of motion, to find the combined speed right after the dart embeds, then use this speed in the centripetal force formula.

A sudden impulse of 20 kg m/s is applied to the system through the front block, giving it an initial speed. Using \( v^2=v_0^2-2as \) with \( v=0 \): \( 0=4^2-2\times2\times s \), so \( s=\dfrac{16}{4}=4 \) m.

questions.question: A conical pendulum consists of a 1 kg ball on a string making a constant \( 37° \) angle with the vertical, moving at constant speed. A brief tangential impulse of 1.5 kg m/s, in the direction of motion and not toward the center, is applied to the ball. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \), what is the tension in the string immediately after this tangential impulse, assuming the angle with the vertical has not yet had time to change?
options: 12.5 N — the tangential impulse does not affect the tension at this instant, since the vertical equilibrium, which determines the tension here, does not depend on the ball's tangential speed
12.5 N plus an additional term from the impulse, giving approximately 14 N
The tension cannot be determined without knowing the new speed and using the full centripetal force equation
9 N, since the tangential impulse reduces the effective weight supported by the string
questions.explanation:
In a conical pendulum, the vertical equilibrium equation \( T\cos\theta=mg \) determines the tension using only the string's angle — it does not involve the ball's speed at all.

A tangential impulse changes the ball's speed but has no component along the string's direction, so it does not instantaneously affect this vertical balance.

So immediately after the tangential impulse, the tension is unchanged: \( T=\dfrac{mg}{\cos37°}=\dfrac{1\times10}{4/5}=12.5 \) N.
questions.hint: Think about which equation actually determines the tension in a conical pendulum — does it involve the ball's speed at all?
distractor_logic: Incorrectly assumes the tangential impulse must add to the tension, when it has no component along the string's direction and does not affect the instantaneous vertical force balance.
Overlooks that the vertical equilibrium equation, \( T\cos\theta=mg \), by itself already determines the tension using only the angle, independent of the ball's speed.
A tangential impulse has no vertical component and cannot reduce the weight that the string's vertical component of tension must support.

questions.question: In the same setup as before — a 3 kg block on a \( 37° \) incline (\( \mu_s=0.6 \)) connected by a string over a pulley to a 1 kg hanging block, the system at rest (\( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \)) — what is the magnitude of the force the incline block exerts on the incline surface, by Newton's third law?
questions.explanation:
The normal force on the block is determined by the component of its weight perpendicular to the incline: \( N=mg\cos37°=3\times10\times\tfrac45=24 \) N.

By Newton's third law, the block exerts an equal and opposite force of 24 N on the incline surface, directed into the incline.
questions.hint: First find the normal force on the block using only the component of its weight perpendicular to the incline, then recall that a genuine third-law reaction pair is always exactly equal in magnitude to the original force.

Uses \( mg\sin37° \), the component of weight along the incline, instead of \( mg\cos37° \), the component perpendicular to the incline, when finding the normal force.

questions.question: A 2 kg ball attached to a string of length 0.8 m moves in a vertical circle. At the topmost point, its speed is 4 m/s. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the magnitude of the force the ball exerts on the string at this topmost point, by Newton's third law?
questions.explanation:
At the topmost point, both gravity and tension point toward the center (downward), so \( T+mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \), giving \( T=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}-mg=\dfrac{2\times16}{0.8}-2\times10=40-20=20 \) N.

This is the force the string exerts on the ball, toward the center.

By Newton's third law, the ball exerts an equal and opposite force of 20 N on the string, directed outward, away from the center.
questions.hint: At the top of the loop, both gravity and tension point toward the center; find the tension first, then apply Newton's third law for the direction of the reaction force.
distractor_logic: Adds the weight to the centripetal force term instead of subtracting it, as though both contributed in the same direction to the tension at the top of the loop.
Uses only the centripetal force term as the tension, forgetting that at the top of the loop, gravity itself already supplies part of the required centripetal force.
Gets the correct magnitude but assigns the wrong direction; this is the direction of the string's force on the ball, not the ball's reaction force on the string, which points outward.

questions.question: A 1000 kg car takes a flat, unbanked curve of radius 50 m at 10 m/s. The maximum static friction available is 6000 N. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the magnitude of the force the car's tires exert on the road due to friction, by Newton's third law?
questions.explanation:
The required centripetal force is \( \dfrac{mv^2}{r}=\dfrac{1000\times10^2}{50}=2000 \) N, well below the maximum available friction of 6000 N.

Since static friction self-adjusts to provide exactly what is needed, the actual friction force the road exerts on the car is 2000 N, not the maximum.

By Newton's third law, the car's tires exert an equal and opposite force of 2000 N on the road.
questions.hint: Just like on a straight road, static friction on a curve self-adjusts to provide only the force actually needed, up to its maximum limit; then apply Newton's third law.
distractor_logic: Uses the maximum available friction instead of recognizing that static friction self-adjusts to provide only the actual force needed, here well below the maximum.
Uses the car's full weight instead of the actual required centripetal force to determine the friction and hence the reaction force.
Doubles the correctly computed centripetal force, rather than using \( mv^2/r \) directly.

Friction: Static, Kinetic, and the Angle of Repose

questions.question: An 11 kg object moves along a banked circular track of angle \( 37° \) (\( \sin37°=\tfrac35 \), \( \cos37°=\tfrac45 \)), where \( \mu_s=0.5 \), at exactly the minimum speed needed to prevent it from sliding down the slope. At this minimum speed, friction acts at its maximum value, up the slope. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is the normal force on the object at this minimum speed?
questions.explanation:
At the minimum speed, friction acts up the slope at its maximum value, \( f=\mu_sN \), which has both a horizontal and vertical component.

Vertical equilibrium gives \( N\cos37°+f\sin37°=mg \), so \( N(\cos37°+\mu_s\sin37°)=mg \).

Substituting: \( N(0.8+0.5\times0.6)=11\times10 \), so \( N\times1.1=110 \), giving \( N=\dfrac{110}{1.1}=100 \) N.
questions.hint: At the minimum speed, friction acts at its maximum value, up the slope, and its vertical component also helps support part of the object's weight — set up the full vertical equilibrium equation with both \( N \) and \( f=\mu_sN \).
distractor_logic: Reports the object's weight directly as the normal force, without accounting for how friction, acting up the slope with a vertical component, also helps support part of the weight.
Uses \( mg\cos37° \) alone, as if this were an ordinary incline with no friction contribution to the vertical direction, instead of including the vertical component of friction as well.
Divides the weight by \( \cos37° \) alone, ignoring the additional friction term entirely in the vertical equilibrium equation.

questions.question: A block sits on a rotating horizontal disk at a distance of 6 m from the center, starting from rest. The disk provides the block with a constant tangential acceleration of 8 m/s\(^2\), and the coefficient of static friction between block and disk is \( \mu_s=1 \). Friction must simultaneously supply both the tangential force and the centripetal force needed, and their combined resultant cannot exceed \( \mu_smg \). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), how long after starting does the block begin to slip?
questions.explanation:
At the moment slipping begins, \( \left(\dfrac{v^2}{r}\right)^2+a_t^2=(\mu_sg)^2 \).

Substituting \( a_t=8 \) m/s\(^2\), \( \mu_sg=10 \) m/s\(^2\): \( \left(\dfrac{v^2}{6}\right)^2=100-64=36 \), so \( \dfrac{v^2}{6}=6 \), giving \( v^2=36 \) and \( v=6 \) m/s.

Starting from rest with constant tangential acceleration, the time to reach this speed is \( t=\dfrac{v}{a_t}=\dfrac{6}{8}=0.75 \) s.
questions.hint: At the moment of slipping, the combined resultant of the tangential and centripetal requirements must exactly equal the maximum available friction; use this to first find the speed at which slipping begins, then find the time to reach that speed.
distractor_logic: Checks only the centripetal requirement against the maximum friction, ignoring the tangential contribution entirely, before finding the speed and time.
Uses only the maximum available friction directly as the speed at which slipping begins, without properly relating it to the actual combined centripetal and tangential requirements.
Checks only the tangential requirement against the full maximum friction, without ever accounting for the additional centripetal force that friction must simultaneously supply as speed increases.
